articles.title: SHOCK POLL: Powerful blue state gov's lead shrinks to single digits weeks before election
articles.summary: Bruce Blakeman trails Kathy Hochul by just nine points in a new Siena poll, closing the gap in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans two-to-one.
articles.body:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman has cut his deficit to Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul to single digits in New York State, with Hochul at 50% support and Blakeman at 41% according to a recent Siena College poll.

Blakeman is doing better with Republicans, leading 88-8%, than Hochul is with Democrats, leading 81-11%, and is also edging Hochul among independent voters 44%-39%.

Despite Hochul leading in another poll by 19 points, two-thirds of New York State voters, including 37% of Republicans, think she will win re-election, while half of likely voters, including a quarter of Republicans, view President Trump's endorsement of Blakeman negatively.

Democrats outnumber Republicans by a roughly two-to-one margin in blue-leaning New York State, but a new poll indicates Republican gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman has cut his deficit to Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul to single digits with just six weeks to go until Election Day .

Hochul, who is running for a second full four-year term steering the nation's fourth most populous state, stands at 50% support among likely voters in New York , with Blakeman at 41%, according to a Siena College poll conducted Sept. 11-17 and released on Wednesday.

Blakeman, the Nassau County executive on New York's Long Island, trailed Hochul by 10 points in Siena's August survey. The one-point movement by Blakeman, who is aiming to become the first Republican in nearly a quarter-century to win an election for governor in New York, is within the survey's margin of error.

"With six weeks until election day, voters offer good news to both Hochul and Blakeman. She now has the support of 50% of voters and saw her favorability and job approval ratings edge into positive territory. He now trails by single digits – well, nine points – in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than two-to-one," Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said.

Greenberg noted that at this point four years ago, Hochul held a 17-point lead over then-Rep. Lee Zeldin, the GOP nominee. But Zeldin closed the gap and ended up losing to Hochul by only six points in the 2022 election.

"Currently, Blakeman is doing a better job with Republicans, leading 88-8%, than Hochul is with Democrats, leading 81-11%," Greenberg added.

The GOP nominee is also edging Hochul 44%-39% among independent voters.

"All polls continue to show Kathy Hochul's downward spiral and me closing the gap as New Yorkers learn more about my plan to cut income taxes by historic margins and slash electric bills in half," Blakeman argued in a statement after the release of the Siena poll.

But the new poll indicates that two-thirds of New York State voters, including 37% of Republicans, think Hochul will win re-election.

Meanwhile, a Quinnipiac University poll also released Wednesday indicated Hochul leading by 19 points, 58% to 39% over Blakeman.

Blakeman is a strong supporter of President Donald Trump , who in February endorsed his bid for governor. But Trump's support may be doing Blakeman no favors, with half of likely voters, including a quarter of Republicans, saying it's a negative for the GOP nominee's campaign.

Hochul was endorsed earlier this year by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , the first socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, reciprocating her backing during his own historic mayoral run last year.

By a 50%-30% margin, voters said Mamdani's support for Hochul is a plus for the governor's bid for re-election.

Then-Lt. Gov. Hochul was sworn in as New York's first female governor in August 2021 after Gov. Andrew Cuomo, in the middle of his third term, resigned amid multiple scandals.

Hochul has seen her political standing rise over the past year and a half as she's increased her resistance to Trump's unprecedented second-term agenda.

Asked about the poll, Hochul campaign spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki, referring to Blakeman, told Fox News Digital, " No one wants a Trump puppet in the governor's mansion who will cut their healthcare, raise their costs, and let ICE trample their rights."

"They trust Governor Hochul's record of investing in public safety, lowering crime, and putting money back in their pockets – and they know she'll fight for their families, not Trump," he added.

The poll, which was conducted by telephone and text-to-web collection, surveyed 1,144 likely voters in New York, with an overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 percentage points for core questions.

articles.title: Trump rolled back regulations for oil company campaign donors, Democrats say
articles.summary: By Richard Cowan and Timothy Gardner WASHINGTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Two top Democrats in the US Senate launched a report on Thursday saying that oil and gas...
articles.body:
Senators Hold Press Conferences Following Weekly Luncheons

WASHINGTON, Sept 24 (Reuters) - Two top Democrats in the US Senate launched a report on Thursday saying that oil and gas companies ‌were rewarded with tax breaks, subsidies and rollbacks of environmental regulation after then-candidate Donald ‌Trump asked them for $1 billion in donations during the 2024 campaign.

The report by Senators Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, ​and Sheldon Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment committee, was based on 19 investigations of regulatory rollbacks by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 13 investigations into nine other agencies and 13 probes into what they called 88 polluters.

The report says that hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending that ‌it tracked after Trump's ask of ⁠the energy companies resulted in hundreds of billions of dollars in tax breaks and revenues as the policies pushed consumers to purchase more fossil fuels.

"Working ⁠families foot the bill, through higher energy prices, weakened public services, and the long-term costs of climate and health damage, while Big Oil executives and shareholders reap the rewards," the report said. "This is, at ​its core, ​a massive transfer of wealth."

The report could be ​a window into what issues Democratic lawmakers ‌will hold hearings on should they take control of the Senate in November's midterm elections. The senators will hold a press conference on the report at 9:45 a.m. ET.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rodgers refuted the report.

"These Democrat Senators should do some self-reflection on their ties to the so-called 'green' energy industry. They wasted billions of American taxpayer dollars in the name of the Green New ‌Scam," Rodgers said.

In the administration's latest move to dismantle ​environmental regulations, the EPA this month announced rules to ​repeal former President Joe Biden's limits on ​carbon emissions from coal and gas-fired power plants and to prevent future ‌climate-focused regulations on them. The moves are ​part of Trump's efforts to ​unwind US climate policy that his administration says has hindered energy production.

The EPA said the move would save the industry hundreds of millions in compliance costs, while the Biden ​administration said its rule would ‌result in hundreds of billion in benefits, including reduced medical bills for health problems ​caused by smog and other emissions.

(Reporting by Timothy Gardner; Additional reporting by Valerie ​Volcovici; Editing by Kevin Buckland and Nick Zieminski)

articles.title: 'Mensagens isoladas não podem ser analisadas fora de contexto', diz relator ao votar contra apuração de Gonet | G1
articles.standfirst: Relator também disse que há apenas mensagens indiretas que citam o procurador-geral. Inclusive, que o contato de Gonet sequer está salvo no celular de Daniel Vorcaro.
articles.summary: Relator também disse que há apenas mensagens indiretas que citam o procurador-geral. Inclusive, que o contato de Gonet sequer está salvo no celular de Daniel Vorcaro.
articles.body:
O relator do processo no Conselho Superior do Ministério Público Federal (CSMPF), subprocurador-geral da República Francisco Sanseverino, votou nesta sexta-feira (25) pelo indeferimento do pedido de designação de um subprocurador-geral para analisar as representações contra o procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet , relacionadas ao caso Banco Master.

“Desde logo, eu voto pelo indeferimento do pedido de designação de subprocurador-geral da República para conhecer da documentação antes mencionada”, afirmou Sanseverino. O relator ainda apresenta os fundamentos do voto.

Sanseverino afirmou que, para dar início a uma investigação criminal, é necessário haver elementos mínimos de materialidade e autoria.

Ao analisar as mensagens extraídas do celular de Daniel Vorcaro, Sanseverino destacou que não há, no material analisado, registro de comunicação direta entre o ex-banqueiro e Paulo Gonet.

As referências ao nome do procurador-geral aparecem em conversas entre Vorcaro e o advogado Ciro Soares.

“Não se pode examinar frases ou troca de mensagens de forma isolada ou descontextualizada para não criar uma situação artificial e que não corresponde à realidade dos fatos”, afirmou o relator.

Antes de entrar na análise do caso concreto, Sanseverino rejeitou analisar, no Conselho, eventual impedimento ou suspeição de Gonet nos processos que tramitam no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ). Segundo o relator, essa questão deve ser decidida pelo próprio Supremo.

“Portanto, não conheço a alegação de impedimento ou suspeição do procurador-geral da República”, disse.

A sessão do Conselho Superior do MPF ocorre nesta sexta-feira (25) e deve decidir sobre a abertura ou não de uma investigação sobre a atuação de Gonet em episódios relacionados ao caso do extinto Banco Master.

➡️ A sessão é presidida pelo vice-presidente do colegiado, subprocurador-geral Nicolao Dino. Embora seja o presidente nato do Conselho, Gonet não participa da reunião por figurar como alvo do procedimento.

A deliberação é inédita na história do órgão e tem como base referências ao chefe do Ministério Público Federal encontradas em relatórios da Polícia Federal.

🔎 O Conselho Superior do MPF é um órgão composto pelos nove integrantes da cúpula da instituição.

Na pauta desta sexta, os conselheiros discutem se as referências ao nome de Paulo Gonet contêm elementos suficientes para justificar o aprofundamento de uma investigação criminal e disciplinar ou se o procedimento deve ser arquivado.

A análise abrange a conduta do procurador-geral sob três eixos principais:

a atuação em relação à prisão preventiva do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro;

a condução geral das apurações do caso Banco Master no âmbito do MPF.

Delegados da PF pedem que Paulo Gonet se declare impedido de atuar em apuração sobre mensagens de Daniel Vorcaro — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Presidência: a reunião é comandada pelo vice-presidente do Conselho, subprocurador-geral da República Nicolao Dino.

Votação do vice-PGR: o vice-procurador-geral da República, Hindenburgo Chateaubriand, participa normalmente das deliberações e do voto.

Relatoria: o relator do procedimento, subprocurador-geral da República Francisco Sanseverino, abre os trabalhos apresentando seu parecer.

Ordem dos votos: após o voto do relator, a votação segue a ordem de antiguidade no conselho, votando primeiro o conselheiro mais novo até o mais antigo.

Daniel Vorcaro e o procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, em Londres — Foto: Reprodução/Jornal O Globo

Próximos passos em caso de abertura de investigação

Se a maioria dos conselheiros votar pela abertura de investigação, um subprocurador-geral da República será designado para conduzir a apuração de forma independente. O designado analisará os dados e apresentará um relatório final ao próprio Conselho.

Caso sejam identificados indícios de crime, os fatos serão encaminhados ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), foro competente para decidir sobre a eventual abertura de inquérito contra o chefe do MPF.

A análise no Conselho do MPF ocorre após a divulgação de relatórios da Polícia Federal produzidos a partir da extração de dados do celular de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, apreendido durante a Operação Compliance Zero .

As mensagens recuperadas pela perícia da PF indicam a existência de interlocução entre o banqueiro e o procurador-geral, realizada majoritariamente por meio do advogado Ciro Soares . Entre os pontos mapeados nos relatórios estão:

Viagem a Londres: registros de mensagens apontam que Daniel Vorcaro autorizou o custeio de despesas de viagem a Londres para Pedro Gonet, filho do procurador-geral, em abril de 2025.

Foto em confraternização: a divulgação de uma fotografia tirada em 2024 em Londres , na qual Vorcaro aparece sentado próximo a Paulo Gonet — que segura um charuto em frente a uma mesa com copos de uísque —, motivou manifestações internas no Ministério Público.

Articulação no CNPG: aiálogos de abril de 2024 mostram o advogado Ciro Soares afirmando a Vorcaro que pediu a intervenção de Gonet para convencer o procurador Georges Seigneur a desistir da disputa pela presidência do Conselho Nacional dos Procuradores-Gerais (CNPG). Três dias após os diálogos, Seigneur retirou a candidatura, e Jarbas Soares foi eleito por aclamação.

Mensagens sobre interlocução institucional: e m mensagens de outubro de 2025, Vorcaro citou o procurador-geral ao pedir a um interlocutor que reforçasse conversas com autoridades para evitar medidas do Banco Central contra a instituição financeira.

O posicionamento de Paulo Gonet e as avaliações no colegiado

Em manifestações anteriores, o procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, declarou não ter relacionamento de proximidade com Daniel Vorcaro e afirmou que o contato mantido com o banqueiro foi "brevíssima e banal".

Paralelamente, a Procuradoria-Geral da República apresentou manifestação ao STF defendendo a anulação do relatório elaborado pela Polícia Federal sob a relatoria do ministro André Mendonça.

Gonet argumentou que o ministro relator extrapolou suas competências ao determinar apurações sem pedido prévio do Ministério Público.

Nos bastidores do Ministério Público Federal, a sessão divide opiniões. Aliados da gestão do PGR avaliam que a maioria do Conselho deve votar pelo arquivamento da apuração.

Por outro lado, conselheiros críticos sustentam que os fatos trazidos a público exigem esclarecimentos formais.

Resumo do caso Banco Master e os desdobramentos no Judiciário

A crise do Banco Master começou com apurações da Polícia Federal e do Banco Central sobre supostas fraudes na cessão de carteiras de crédito estimadas em R$ 12 bilhões, culminando na decretação de liquidação extrajudicial da instituição em novembro de 2025.

O ex-dono do banco Master Daniel Vorcaro foi preso preventivamente no aeroporto de Guarulhos enquanto tentava embarcar para o exterior.

A derrubada do sigilo de relatórios da PF pelo relator no STF, ministro André Mendonça, expôs trocas de mensagens e registros de encontros de Vorcaro com diferentes autoridades da República.

Além das referências a Paulo Gonet, o documento detalhou interações do ex-banqueiro com o ministro Alexandre de Moraes e a existência de contratos de prestação de serviços com o escritório da advogada Viviane Barci de Moraes, esposa do ministro.

articles.title: Lula reforça críticas às bets: 'Não é correto gastar o que não tem' | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente anuncia nesta sexta-feira (25), em São Paulo, um pacote de medidas econômicas, que deve incluir medidas contra bets e contra o endividamento das famílias.
articles.summary: Lula e as bets: presidente anuncia medidas contra o endividamento das famílias e o vício em apostas online em pacote econômico nesta sexta.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) reforçou, nesta sexta-feira (25), as críticas que tem feito sobre as apostas online. Em um ato de campanha no Recife (PE), o petista afirmou que "o dinheiro do jogo é para comprar a comida das crianças".

"O dinheiro do jogo é pra comida das crianças, se quiser jogar, compra um litro de leite pra sua casa, pão, mais comida pra sua casa, Não é correto gastar o que não tem pra tentar ganhar o que não existe, não da pra acreditar em mentira", disse Lula.

Lula anuncia nesta sexta-feira (25), em São Paulo, um pacote de medidas econômicas, que deve incluir medidas contra bets e contra o endividamento das famílias.

A expectativa é que o governo proíba o funcionamento de empresas de apostas no Brasil. Durante atos de campanha em diversos estados, ao longo da semana, o petista tem endurecido as críticas às apostas e ao vício.

Lula com o candidato ao governo de PE João Campos em evento no Recife — Foto: Foto: Ricardo Stuckert.

A expectativa é que a mudança seja anunciada por meio de Medida Provisória. Órgãos do Executivo já estão organizando ações internamente partindo do pressuposto de que a MP será publicada a qualquer momento.

Devem participar do evento o ministro do governo que participaram das discussões sobre as mudanças no tema, como Dario Durigan (Fazenda) e Miriam Belchior (Casa Civil).

Nesta quarta-feira (23), o presidente se reuniu com ministros de seu governo para discutir medidas para restrição das bets.

Estavam presentes os ministros Dario Durigan, da Fazenda, Miriam Belchior, da Casa Civil, Bruno Moretti, do Orçamento e Planejamento, Wellignton César, da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Sidônio Palmeira, da Secretaria de Comnicação, e o presidente do Banco Central, Gabriel Galípolo.

O presidente já decidiu que quer fazer o anúncio sobre o fim das bets, mas há uma divisão na equipe entre uma proibição total das apostas ou uma medida de impacto superficial, como vetar publicidades e proibir cassinos virtuais, como o "Jogo do Tigrinho".

articles.title: Justice Jackson says Supreme Court intervenes too quickly on Trump's side
articles.summary: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warns that emergency appeals are becoming a "special avenue" for "certain privileged litigants."
articles.body:
WASHINGTON − Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson continued her ongoing criticism of how her colleagues are handling emergency appeals, telling an audience on Sept. 24 that requests for immediate intervention can't become a "special avenue that certain privileged litigants can use selectively."

"As one of my colleagues recently suggested in an opinion," Jackson said during remarks at the University of the District of Columbia law school, "some frequent emergency docket filers have the court on speed dial."

Although Jackson never mentioned the Trump administration, she was referring to Justice Sonia Sotomayor's dissent last year when the conservative court backed the administration in a dispute with a federal judge over the administration's attempt to deport eight migrants to South Sudan.

In her own opinions, Jackson − one of the three liberal justices − has complained that the court is showing preferential treatment for the government, along with a willingness to undercut lower court judges.

She did so last year when the court allowed the administration to block $783 million in grants for health research.

"This is Calvinball jurisprudence with a twist," Jackson wrote , referring to a made-up game in the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes. "Calvinball has only one rule: There are no fixed rules. We seem to have two: that one, and this Administration always wins."

The rulings she referenced came on emergency requests from the administration to let a controversial policy move forward while it's being challenged in court.

When major policies of President Donald Trump have come before the justices for a final ruling, the court permanently shut down his attempts to use emergency powers to impose tariffs and to rewrite citizenship rules .

But a majority has more often than not sided with the president on the interim decisions about Trump's policies that are decided without a full record or oral arguments.

Jackson said the Supreme Court didn't use to get involved as often in the early stages of the litigation. Instead, the justices "waited humbly until the facts were established and the lower courts had fully and fairly assessed the law."

"It was only in exigent circumstances, actual emergencies, that the justices felt the need to intervene in pending cases," she said. "I think the justices understood that very little good comes from taking an institution that is supposed to be operating outside of the political realm and routinely steering it into the fray."

But in recent years, Jackson said, the court "has been noticeably less restrained, especially with respect to pending cases that involve controversial matters."

In those cases, Jackson said, anyone seeking the court's early help should have to show that something harmful is about to happen "in the real world" without intervention.

If they can do that, then the justices should issue a ruling based on which side will experience the greater harm.

"We have an appellate review process with an equitable emergency exception that can sometimes warrant the Supreme Court's early intervention, but only when exigent circumstances require it," she said. "I feel strongly that we should be sticking to that history and tradition."

articles.title: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.summary: The party projects confidence, but the Sunshine State isn’t immune to voter anger over high prices, the war in Iran and mass deportations.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is not making it easy for Republicans in Florida to keep their firewall.

The same forces undercutting the GOP in other states — including Trump's war in Iran and ensuing high gas prices, Hispanic voters turned off by his immigration surges and stubborn concerns over affordability — are hitting Floridians.

Now, some polling has shown statewide races inside the margin of error, including for governor and U.S. Senate. Democratic congressional seats seen as flippable after mid-decade redistricting are a question mark while some Republicans have distanced themselves from an increasingly unpopular president.

Democratic wins in Florida would send tremors through the political ecosystem. It could not only help increase Democrats' margins if they win back the House, but would also have a dramatic impact on the 2028 presidential race if Democrats win the governor's race, given Florida has 30 electoral college votes up for grabs. Both Gov. Ron DeSantis and Trump won landslide victories in 2022 and 2024.

Few top Republicans are publicly panicking about losing statewide seats, especially since Democrats have much less money and a history of electoral missteps. But POLITICO heard emerging concerns in interviews with nearly two dozen GOP politicians, operatives and consultants — many of whom acknowledged Republicans shouldn't take a win in the Sunshine State for granted.

"It's definitely 2018 vibes out there," said Carlos Curbelo, a former Florida GOP House member who lost his reelection during Democrats' 2018 blue wave during Trump's first presidency. "A lot of former colleagues are bracing for the worst."

"I still bet on Republicans holding the governor's mansion," he continued, "but it's going to be more competitive than people could have anticipated just a few months ago."

Added GOP state Sen. Don Gaetz: "Anybody who is on the ballot ought to be concerned if they have a Democratic opponent." Gaetz, father of former Rep. Matt Gaetz, hails from northwest Florida, which has been called "victory lane" for Republicans in the state.

The fundamentals in Florida unquestionably favor Republicans. The Republican candidate for governor, Rep. Byron Donalds , has raised nearly $121 million, which is more than 10 times the amount of his Democratic opponent, former Rep. David Jolly. Republicans have a 1.55 million voter registration advantage over Democrats. National groups aren't rushing in to help.

Republicans also see themselves as having an ideological advantage since the Democratic Senate nominee, state Rep. Angie Nixon of Jacksonville, is an insurgent progressive candidate who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June. They confidently predict her positions will repel influential voters in South Florida whose families fled left-wing dictatorships in Cuba, Venezuela and Nicaragua.

But there are shifts in Democrats' favor. A New York Times analysis found Hispanic voters are moving to the left, an erosion of Trump's winning 2024 coalition. A Fox News poll published findings this week that show several Florida House races moving from "Likely R" to "Lean R" or even "Lean R" to "Toss-up." Decision Desk HQ, an independent elections forecasting organization, rates the governor's race as a "toss up."

"I don't think we are dead yet," said one GOP county chair in Florida, granted anonymity to speak candidly as the party both nationally and in state has dismissed any possible concerns about the state of play. "We are not on life support. But we are hemorrhaging. The question is: Do we stop the bleeding now, or wait until we reach critical conditions?"

Several factors appear to be undercutting the GOP advantage, including the effects of Trump's mass deportations. Rep. María Elvira Salazar , a Miami Republican and daughter of Cuban exiles in a competitive reelection contest, launched a TV ad last week complaining they'd "gone too far." And as Cubans and Venezuelans await changes to their home countries' regimes, Trump has been photographed this week smiling next to Democratic socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and meeting with interim Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodríguez.

Tony Figueroa, president of Miami Young Republicans, which operates separately from the Republican Party of Florida, said he didn't think populous Miami-Dade County was guaranteed for Republicans, noting Democrats control the city and county mayors' offices.

"We can never rest on our laurels just because of our gains with DeSantis and Trump," he said. "They're not on the ballot, and given everything that has gone on in the past two years — Trump was elected on affordability, and we are still talking about it two years later, it's never a given."

Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, cited Trump's record on jobs, national security, energy, the cost of drugs and boosting the value of the investment accounts of Americans as a reason that Republicans would win in the midterms.

"President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party," Ingle said. "The choice has never been clearer: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction."

Yet the picture of the electorate in Florida specifically gets murkier when factoring in the partisan fault lines that have emerged over data centers, with Democrats at the top of the ticket firmly against their construction. And separately, a scandal has erupted over $10 million in "misappropriated" taxpayer money that has entangled GOP Sen. Ashley Moody and Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, two DeSantis appointees who are up for election in November.

Also, the GOP voter registration advantage may not be as solid as it appears. An analysis of voter registration conducted by a GOP consultant shows that more than 70% of 5.6 million registered Republicans were enrolled with the party in 2022, the year that DeSantis won his reelection by almost 20 points. Nearly all the growth since then has come from people who switched from Democrat or were not signed up with any party.

Mason-Dixon Pollster Brad Coker of Jacksonville called those voters potentially "squishy." He noted many of them moved from blue states to Florida during and after the throes of the Covid pandemic because they liked having few restrictions. But a good chunk may not necessarily be GOP devotees and could prove to be a "wildcard" during the coming election, perhaps affecting the governor's race.

"I can't sit here and say Jolly can't win," he continued. "That to me is definitely possible. But the odds are Donalds wins."

The Senate contest has its own complications. Though Nixon's progressive positions risk repelling certain segments of the electorate, she's also a charismatic grassroots campaigner expected to appeal to Black voters, young people and progressives. If she's able to pull in those groups — who weren't energized in the last two cycles — other Democrats could benefit.

Moody, in contrast, has run a very cautious campaign , one whose posture has members of her own party grimly likening it to that of former President Joe Biden. Her campaign started airing TV ads against Nixon this week, though AdImpact shows they're concentrated in the political battleground I-4 corridor that extends from Tampa in the west to Daytona Beach in the east rather than in Cuban and Venezuelan diaspora-heavy South Florida.

Brandon Ludwig, who chairs Florida Young Republicans and lives in northeast Florida, has been canvassing statewide in a bid to juice turnout among base voters. He told POLITICO those voters raise Nixon's DSA associations and tend to want candidates who side closely with the president — underscoring Trump's continued staying power with the base in his adopted home state.

"Florida is safe red," Ludwig said, "but if you get complacent and don't engage with those voters, then that advantage doesn't bring them out. We are working on voters that may not vote."

Political strategist Alex Patton said his research shows the electorate in Florida appears angrier than he has seen in a long time, which could increase the chances of "lighting in a bottle" for Democrats. Patton left the GOP a couple of years ago due to the Trump takeover of the party and is now an independent.

"The perfect storm exists for Democratic surprises," he said, pointing to "an arrogant GOP that thinks they can't lose" as well as "national trends tanking."

But Donalds brushed off the polling shifts, attributing them to "the overall national environment." He added, however, that in traveling the state he'd seen voters wanted Florida to stay the course.

"People love Florida," Donalds said. "Our Democrats love Florida. Independents love Florida. Republicans — obviously. … People have chosen our state for a reason, and my belief is that they're going to choose the same direction, the same kind of common sense this November."

Donalds' race appears to be tightening despite his political committee and the Republican Party spending nearly $80 million on ads, according to ad tracker AdImpact. As a candidate, Donalds has been flooding the zone with campaign events, which are broadcast through his social media. In contrast, Jolly has refused to debate. He became a Democrat just last year and his even-tempered demeanor clashes with a large segment of a base brimming with fury.

Yet five Republicans interviewed for this story said they'd be concerned about the race if Jolly were able to raise even $20 million. Many point to losses Donalds, who is Black, faced during his primary in 17 heavily white and rural counties.

"If [Democrats] had fielded a better candidate there would be more concern," said one long-time Florida Republican consultant who was granted anonymity to discuss the climate candidly.

Another GOP operative, who was also granted anonymity to talk frankly about the upcoming election, said about the governor's race that "the big fear is that a weird tech bro could get in, but the Democratic megadonors are more focused on the federal level." That operative said "anything can happen but the math is the math."

Many Republican officials are publicly dismissive that Democrats have a shot at Florida. Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, contended that Democrats are "doomed" and that Democrats are "living in a fever dream" if they think they can win.

While the National Republican Senatorial Committee appears to be pulling its focus back from Senate seats in North Carolina and Georgia, alarm bells about Florida are nowhere to be found. Nick Puglia, NRSC regional press secretary, argued Florida voters wouldn't let Nixon "turn the Free State into another failed socialist experiment." He predicted voters would back Moody given she supported the Trump tax cuts and because of her record on law enforcement as a former state attorney general. Moody's allies in Florida also note that, as state attorney general, she won statewide twice by higher margins than other Republicans on the ticket, a trend they expect in her Senate race.

Evan Power, chair of the Republican Party of Florida, said that while the midterms are "challenging" he noted past predictions of a Democratic wave in the state never materialized.

"I take nothing for granted, but I'm not raising alarms," Power said. "I think our voters are going to come home. We are going to turn out voters."

articles.title: WATCH: Mike Lee explodes on voting error that 'keeps happening' as huge number of noncitizens found on rolls
articles.summary: Mike Lee railed against noncitizen voting after a report found 30,000 noncitizens were mistakenly added to voter rolls since 2000 across 11 states.
articles.body: Firebrand conservative Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, slammed both Democrats and Republicans who have resisted passage of the SAVE America Act after a report found that 30,000 noncitizens were "mistakenly" registered to vote in states across the country since 2000. Reuters reported on Wednesday that more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens have been added to U.S. voter rolls since 2000. The outlet attributed the erroneous registrations to "software glitches and clerical errors" and said that its review suggested "inadvertent bureaucratic failures, ‌rather than organized efforts to register immigrants illegally." The outlet said that this raised "questions about whether legislative efforts to require proof of citizenship for voter registration would eliminate the issue." However, while speaking on the Senate floor on Wednesday, Lee, who introduced the SAVE America Act earlier this year, said that "even though we have laws that prohibit things like noncitizen voting, those laws have been rendered difficult and essentially impossible to enforce." "That thing that they claim never happens, voter fraud or noncitizen voting, just keeps happening over and over and over again," he railed. ‘RAW MATERIAL FOR ELECTION FRAUD’: EXPERT FLAGS VOTER-ROLL PROBLEMS FAR BEYOND ONE STATE Reuters reported that the errors occurred in California, Illinois, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and Virginia. The outlet said it was unable to determine how many noncitizens actually cast ballots and further noted that the numbers are not precise because "state data is often tentative and subject to revision." This follows New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's disclosure that 6,600 self-identified noncitizens were registered to vote and fewer than 400 of those individuals cast ballots. Lee attributed problems with ineligible voter registration and voting to reliance on the "honor system" for self-attestation of voter eligibility. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Referencing an all-you-can-eat deal at a popular chain restaurant that requires customers to show I.D., Lee said that "it should not be any easier for someone to get away with voter fraud at a polling location on voting day than it is to cheat Olive Garden through its never-ending pasta pass." "And yet, that's exactly where we are today," he said. Lee presented his SAVE America Act as a solution. President Donald Trump supports the bill, which passed the House but has stalled in the Senate. RNC SUES NEW JERSEY ELECTION OFFICIALS OVER ALLEGED WITHHELD VOTER ROLL RECORDS Lee argued that the bill would address both ineligible voter registration and fraudulent voting by requiring registrants to verify citizenship and eligibility at the time of registration and requiring voter ID and photo identification at the polls. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In an interview with Fox News Digital, Don Palmer, senior legal fellow for election integrity at the Heritage Foundation, said that "this story really provides proof that one way forward is to simply upgrade and sort of help the driver's license agencies across the country improve their verification of citizenship while they're providing those services to voters." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "All joking aside with the Olive Garden scenario, I love their food, and I'm more than happy to show the ID. I think the issue is I wish that the driver's license agencies and state agencies would take voter registration as serious as Italian food," he quipped. "I think that that would be a bipartisan way of improving that verification of citizenship with databases, and I think there's some bipartisan support for that. And so that might be a way forward, not necessarily, showing documentation of citizenship, but let's improve the driver's license agencies to verify citizenship, and let's improve REAL ID," he said.

articles.title: Donalds rips opponent’s ‘complete 180’ as Dem’s own 2016 words come back to haunt him in tightening gov race
articles.summary: Byron Donalds attacks David Jolly's shifting stances on abortion, immigration and drilling, calling them political convenience in Florida's governor race.
articles.body: Florida gubernatorial candidate, Republican Congressman Byron Donalds, is taking aim at his Democratic opponent David Jolly over his shifting political positions and party affiliation, in a contest that is resurfacing themes from the 2016 congressional race between Jolly and Charlie Crist. "You were pro-choice, then you were pro-life, then you were pro-choice. It was only after you switched parties that you switched your position. This was not a matter of conviction for you; it was for political convenience," Jolly said about Charlie Crist when Jolly was a Republican running against Crist, a Democrat, for Congress in 2016. Ten years later, Jolly is now a Democrat running for Florida governor and facing the same criticism for allegedly changing his positions for political gain, this time, in his race for governor against Donalds. "The shift in positions by David Jolly is not because of personal conviction, it is purely because of political convenience," Donalds told Fox News Digital, referencing that 2016 exchange. DESANTIS ENDORSES FLORIDA GOP SLATE INCLUDING BYRON DONALDS IN GOVERNOR'S RACE Some of the shifts in Jolly’s positions include issues like abortion, immigration and drilling off the coast of Florida. As a Republican, Jolly said he believed "life begins at conception," authored legislation to defund Planned Parenthood and co-sponsored fetal-personhood legislation. He also voted for a federal 20-week abortion ban. Now running as a Democrat, Jolly calls himself "pro-choice," supports codifying the Roe v. Wade framework and says he would veto legislation restricting abortion access as governor. Jolly’s immigration views have also shifted sharply as he attempts to run for governor in a state that voted for Trump each of the last three presidential cycles by wide margins, with many voters motivated by Trump’s immigration policies. As a Republican, he campaigned on securing the border, supported tighter screening for Syrian and Iraqi refugees and voted for the American SAFE Act. Today, he says the country should have "wide gates" for people coming to work or seek asylum, argues that crossing the border without legal status should not necessarily be treated as a crime in those circumstances and has called the Republican link between immigration and crime "gross," "immoral" and "wrong." As voters consistently say that affordability is a top-of-mind concern, Donalds is also hitting Jolly’s record on healthcare as an example of inconsistency that shows a lack of credibility on the issue. NEVER-TRUMP REPUBLICAN IS TOP DEM CHOICE IN CRUCIAL FLORIDA PRIMARY "When David Jolly was in Congress, he opposed Obamacare," Donalds said. "Now trying to run for governor, he wants to expand Obamacare in Florida. I mean, these are just some of the complete shifts that we've seen in what he stands for." Another issue Donalds is taking issue with involves the period after the devastating Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which sent oil and tar balls washing ashore along roughly 178 miles of Florida coastline, contributed to an estimated loss of 1.88 million planned recreational visits in northwest Florida and cost the region $1.3 billion in visitor spending, $2.04 billion in economic output and more than 20,000 job-years. Within a year of the spill, Jolly’s lobbying firm represented a client that publicly advocated for legislation that could have expanded offshore drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Three Bridges Advisors listed H.R. 909, the Roadmap for America’s Energy Future, among the subjects of its 2011 lobbying activity for the Free Enterprise Nation, which supported the bill. Jolly also wrote a post on the group’s website stating that Free Enterprise Nation was "advocating for" the legislation. BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY' Jolly said he had "never lobbied for offshore drilling," but PolitiFact rated that claim "Mostly False" after finding that Jolly acknowledged attending a meeting where the bill was discussed, which lobbying experts said technically counted as lobbying. Donalds cited the controversy to Fox News Digital saying, "Deepwater Horizon exploded in the Gulf of America, David Jolly went and became a lobbyist for more oil drilling off the coast of Florida, that is a fact and so, what we're seeing is a history of somebody who does everything possible, will say whatever, will be paid by whomever that are only in the interest of David Jolly." With polls showing a tightening race, the RealClearPolitics average gives Donalds a nearly 4-point lead. The candidates are also sparring over debate scheduling: Donalds has agreed to three proposed debates, while Jolly, who previously accepted two other debate invitations, has now ruled out participating in debates this cycle. "Now he's ducking debates," Donalds told Fox News Digital. "He won't debate me because he knows that on a debate stage, I will hold him accountable for these things." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Jolly has hit Donalds on the campaign trail on a variety of issues as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida since Lawton Chiles won re-election in 1994. Primarily, Jolly has focused on data centers and labeled Donalds as a candidate more interested in partisan culture-war battles than addressing Florida’s rising housing, insurance and healthcare costs. Fox News Digital reached out to the Jolly campaign for comment. Donalds told Fox News Digital that Jolly’s flips on both party registration and the issues are things his campaign will continue to focus on. "What you find with David Jolly is somebody who's done a complete 180 simply to run for office again and to gain relevance again and the people of Florida simply cannot trust David Jolly because we cannot afford David Jolly’s flip-flopping when it comes to the great state of Florida," Donalds said.

articles.title: Relator vota contra pedido para investigar Paulo Gonet no caso Master; sessão no conselho do MPF continua
articles.summary: Órgão vai avaliar se menções ao procurador-geral em mensagens de Vorcaro justificam aprofundar a apuração; foto dos dois em confraternização em Londres aumentou críticas internas.
articles.body:
Órgão vai avaliar se menções ao procurador-geral em mensagens de Vorcaro justificam aprofundar a apuração; foto dos dois em confraternização em Londres aumentou críticas internas.

O Conselho Superior do MPF analisa nesta sexta (25) se abre investigação sobre atuação do procurador-geral, Paulo Gonet, no caso Master

O órgão decidirá se arquiva o procedimento ou se há elementos para aprofundar a apuração. Veja como será o rito.

A análise tem como base menções ao chefe do MPF em mensagens do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, dono do Banco Master e preso pelo escândalo financeiro.

A divulgação de uma foto de Gonet com Vorcaro em uma confraternização em Londres ampliou o desgaste interno.

Gonet afirma que não tinha relação de proximidade com o banqueiro e classificou o contato entre ambos como “brevíssimo e banal”.

O relator dividiu a análise. Ele votou contra os pedidos de afastamento de Gonet das investigações do caso Master por questão processual. Com isso, ele vota para manter Gonet à frente do caso Master.

Agora, ele vai analisar eventual cometimento de crime comum por Gonet.

Fala agora o subprocurador-geral Francisco Sanseverino, relator do caso.

Sessão começa. A análise é presidida pelo vice-presidente do colegiado, subprocurador-geral Nicolao Dino. Embora seja o presidente nato do Conselho, Gonet não participa da reunião por figurar como alvo do procedimento.

O Conselho Superior do Ministério Público Federal analisa nesta sexta-feira (25) se há elementos para aprofundar a apuração sobre menções ao procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, em mensagens do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, dono do Banco Master e preso por crimes financeiros. O órgão decidirá pelo arquivamento do procedimento ou pela continuidade da investigação.

A análise ocorre em meio ao desgaste provocado pela divulgação de uma foto de Gonet com Vorcaro em uma confraternização em Londres. O PGR afirma que não tinha relação de proximidade com o banqueiro e classificou o contato entre os dois como “brevíssimo e banal”.

Caso o Conselho entenda que há indícios a serem investigados, um subprocurador-geral da República será designado para analisar o material. Entenda mais sobre o rito.

articles.title: From ‘cheats’ to ‘great friendship’: How Trump’s rhetoric on China changed
articles.summary: Warmth on display in Washington contrasts significantly with the language Trump has used to characterise Beijing and Xi.
articles.body:
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday evening, United States President Donald Trump rolled out a warm and unusually lavish welcome for his Chinese counterpart.

Trump went down to Joint Base Andrews near Washington to greet Xi on the tarmac – the first time a US president has greeted a foreign leader in such a way since 1962, when John F Kennedy welcomed UK Prime Minister Harold Macmillan.

Though the Xi-Trump meeting delivered little significant shift in relations beyond extending a fragile trade war truce for another two months , Washington laid on hours of pageantry, more pomp and lavish tours for Xi’s entourage, and praise for the Chinese president and his wife.

But the warmth on display in Washington this week contrasts starkly with the language Trump has used to characterise Beijing and Xi in the past. We map how the language of communication, and the larger relationship, has changed over a decade.

How has Trump talked about China in the past?

Here are some examples of how Trump addressed Xi and China.

On Twitter, now X, Trump posted: “No surprise that China was caught cheating in the Olympics. That’s the Chinese M.O. – Lie, Cheat & Steal in all international dealings.”

Trump said at a campaign event in South Carolina: “You can win against China if you’re smart. But our people don’t have a clue. We give state dinners to the heads of China. I said, why are you doing state dinners for them? They’re ripping us left and right. Just take them to McDonald’s and go back to the negotiating table.”

In his book, Crippled America: How to Make America Great Again, Trump wrote: “There are people who wish I wouldn’t refer to China as our enemy. But that’s exactly what they are. They have destroyed entire industries by utilizing low-wage workers, cost us tens of thousands of jobs, spied on our businesses, stolen our technology, and have manipulated and devalued their currency, which makes importing our goods more expensive – and sometimes, impossible.”

At an election campaign rally in Indiana, Trump stated: “We can’t continue to allow China to rape our country and that’s what they’re doing. It’s the greatest theft in the history of the world.”

At a Labor Day news conference at the White House, President Trump stated: “ … there’s been no country anywhere, at any time, that’s ripped us off like China has. We’ve lost billions and billions and billions of dollars by dealing with China. And they take that money, and they build their military.”

Speaking with reporters amid the escalating US-China trade war, President Trump said: I don’t blame China at all [for the US losing billions of dollars in trade with Beijing]. I don’t blame President Xi. I like him. He likes me. Who knows? Who the hell cares, frankly. … I don’t blame China. I don’t blame Vietnam. I don’t – I see they’re meeting today. Isn’t – that’s a lovely meeting. They’re meeting, like, trying to figure out, “How do we screw the United States of America?”

Those are just a few of the phrases Trump has used this week to describe Xi and Beijing.

This week’s state visit was the first by a Chinese leader to the US in 11 years. But it is also the third time in less than a year that Trump and Xi have met face to face, as the two powers remain uneasily gridlocked in competition over the development of AI, access to rare-earth metals, the question of Taiwan, and the Iran war.

Overhanging it all is the paused, but simmering, trade war between two nations.

Early into his second term at the White House, Trump upped tariffs on Chinese goods as he accused China of facilitating the flow of fentanyl, a deadly drug, to the US. Beijing responded with its own levies and restricted exports of valuable rare-earth metals, crucial for the development and manufacture of everything high-tech, from smartphones to fighter jets.

At its peak, tariffs headed towards 150 percent by each side before being paused to allow time for talks in October last year.

But nearly a year since the two sides called that temporary truce, the US position is not as strong as China’s, analysts say.

First, despite Trump’s ambition of reducing trade deficits with other countries via his campaign of tariffs, the gap between China and the US has widened – and not in favour of the US .

Washington’s overall trade deficit has remained stagnant and, in fact, risen in some quarters. Between May and July 2025, the US recorded a combined goods trade deficit of about $277bn, according to Census Bureau data. In the same period in 2026, the deficit reached $325bn, an increase of 17.4 percent.

Meanwhile, Beijing has been minting profits. China’s total goods exports rose 6.1 percent in 2025, reaching about $3.77 trillion, according to its National Bureau of Statistics. Until August this year, China had a goods trade surplus of about $820bn – already approaching the mammoth 2025 full-year surplus of roughly $1.2 trillion.

The equation is such that US-China’s bilateral trade has been in a near free-fall over the last two years, just as the US national debt hit a record $40bn this year – two years ahead of expectations.

“Washington is playing a high-stakes game of economic chicken with a $40 trillion debt load, an inflationary sword of Damocles, zero fiscal cushion to absorb a truce collapse and a dependence [on] Chinese industrial and manufacturing inputs,” Beijing-based Einar Tangen, a senior fellow at the Center for International Governance Innovation, told Al Jazeera.

US consumers and the economy in general will find it tough to survive yet another inflationary shock from renewed tariffs “at a time when the federal budget already operates like a high-wire Ponzi scheme,” he added.

Trump simply can’t afford for the trade truce to collapse now.

Second is China’s ace card of rare earth metals. These are crucial for the development of AI and defence sectors as they are used in the manufacture of all things tech, from smartphones to fighter jets. China has 60 percent of the world’s known deposits of these minerals, and processes 90 percent of them. During the trade war last year, China restricted exports of seven of the 12 it has in April, and threatened to restrict five more before the truce delayed that.

China, therefore, has huge leverage and Trump has little choice but to play nice, observers say.

What are the main outcomes from the Xi-Trump summit?

The bottom line is that the meeting in Washington showcased the two nations’ potential for bilateral relations rather than any grand bargain in the making. While the trade truce was extended, major strategic disputes like the question of Taiwan, the war on Iran, as well as tensions over trade and technology remain unresolved.

Trade truce extended: The US and China agreed to extend their existing trade truce, which had been due to expire in November, giving negotiators more time to work towards a broader agreement. The extension now runs to January 10.

No breakthrough on Iran: Trump had wanted Beijing to use its influence with Tehran to help isolate Iran economically and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. No breakthrough was reported.

Taiwan remains unresolved: Xi urged Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the Taiwan issue “prudently”, China’s Xinhua news agency reported. The White House has not commented on it so far; however, a second, $14bn arms deal between the US and Taiwan, following an $11bn sale announced in December last year, remains on hold.

Push for stable relations: Both leaders signalled a desire to prevent further deterioration in ties. Xi called for competition to remain “within bounds” and warned against the “Thucydides Trap” of conflict between a rising and established power.

AI race: In advance of the talks, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington had proposed an AI “ notification mechanism ” with China – in effect, a hotline to alert each other when AI incidents threaten national security.

articles.title: Inside NBC News’ polling averages: Democrats enjoy biggest lead yet in the race for Congress
articles.summary: Meanwhile, President Donald Trump’s approval rating is at a low point for his second term.
articles.body: Democrats are heading into the final stretch of the 2026 midterms with their largest lead yet in the race for Congress and President Donald Trump’s approval rating at a significant low, according to NBC News’ newly released polling averages. A 9-percentage-point advantage for Democrats when it comes to control of Congress is part of a steady deterioration of the political environment for Republicans. The parties started the road to this November effectively tied in the weeks after President Donald Trump returned to office last year, but independents have gradually begun to prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress. And those voters have soured on Trump and his economic policies in particular. The congressional average, which stands at 52% to 43% after adjusting to a likely voter scale, measures whether Americans prefer a Congress controlled by Democrats or Republicans before things like individual races and candidates come into play. Individual polls can bounce around, but an average gives a broad sense of where surveys are trending, and it controls for outliers, which is one reason NBC News released our averages now. At a time when a flurry of polling is released, such as in the homestretch of an election cycle, averages can be valuable tools for tracking what’s happening in the election and diving deeper into how Republicans, Democrats and independents view Trump and the battle for Congress. The NBC News averages are weighted calculations of all publicly available polls that meet certain standards for methodology and transparency tracking back to the beginning of the second Trump administration. With a month to go before the midterm elections, Trump’s approval rating has slid to 39% in the NBC News polling average, with 59% disapproving of his job performance so far. He began his term at 50% approval, according to the average. Independents drive the shift toward Democrats There has been little change over time among partisans in the race for Congress, with the vast majorities of Republicans and Democrats standing with their parties consistently. As a result, much of the shift toward a preference for a Democratic-controlled Congress can be explained by the changing preferences of political independents. Independents preferred Democrats by about 6 points at the beginning of Trump’s second term, and they slowly moved toward Democrats toward the first half of last year. But things began to shift more rapidly during fall 2025 and early 2026, moving to a lead of about 20 points for Democrats in the spring — as public frustration with Trump’s handling of the economy, the war in Iran and the killings of two Americans by federal immigration officers began to boil over. The Republican Party hasn’t fully recovered with independents since, and Democrats now hold a 16-point lead among those voters in the race for Congress, according to the average. While survey responses don’t automatically translate into election results, such a strong showing among political independents is one of the many encouraging signs for Democrats heading into the election. Even so, it’s no guarantee of electoral success for Democrats as Republicans seek to find a way to energize the coalition that sent Trump to the White House just two years ago and narrow the gap before Election Day, more than a month away. Republicans also hope they can defy the political headwinds because so many of the key battleground House and Senate races are being fought in districts and states Trump won in 2024, some by double-digit margins. What’s behind Trump’s low approval rating For Trump, movement among independents — and Republicans, to a lesser extent — explains his low marks from voters. His approval rating among Republicans fluctuated in the mid-to-high 80s for the first six months of his second term, but now, his GOP approval rating is at 79% in a slight but noticeable decline, according to the average. Independents’ approval of Trump has dropped further, to 26% in the NBC News average. Voters have specifically soured on his handling of two of his signature issues — the economy and border security and immigration. In April 2025, an NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey found 40% of American adults approved of Trump’s handling of inflation and the cost of living, while 60% disapproved. By this April’s poll, 32% approved and 68% disapproved. Inside the averages Every polling average reflects decisions about which polls to include, how much influence to give them and how to account for differences in whom pollsters survey and how they go about it. Some polls survey all adults in the U.S., which includes people who aren’t registered to vote or who aren’t eligible to be registered, such as recent immigrants. Other polls specifically survey registered voters. A third set of polls — which become more frequent as the clock ticks down to Election Day — are polls of a population that pollsters identify as likely voters. Likely voter polls try to capture the attitudes of the group of people who will actually cast ballots, a moving target for polling organizations given the impossible task of predicting voter turnout exactly. Those three sample universes produce slightly different results on our two key questions. Polls of all adults consistently show a lower approval rating for Trump compared with polls of registered or likely voters. Likely voters are likelier to have made up their mind on the generic ballot question about control of Congress, and as a result, both parties receive higher vote shares among that group. Both our presidential and congressional averages combine those three universes by adjusting polls of adults and likely voters so they are on the same scale as registered voters. However, because the congressional ballot preference is a question about how people will vote, the congressional average shifts to show a likely voter baseline after Labor Day.

articles.title: GOP handed new lifeline on biggest pocketbook fight of midterms
articles.summary: Club for Growth's memo urges Republicans to blame federal expansion for high cost of living and resist subsidies ahead of the November midterms.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Republicans are being given a new playbook on an issue that is all but certain to be the biggest political lightning rod of the November midterms. Conservative group Club for Growth is sending a memo to Capitol Hill lawmakers on Friday arguing that Americans' struggle with high living costs cannot be ignored — and that the fault lies with an expanding federal government. "Americans are not asking whether the inflation rate has slowed; they are asking why the same basket of goods is permanently more expensive," the information packets being distributed to Republican lawmakers read. "[G]overnment made core costs higher through deficit spending, subsidies, mandates, and restrictions on supply." It's an argument that could be a lifeline for the GOP as it fights an uphill battle to keep control of the House and Senate. While Democrats attack Republicans for how Americans feel about prices today, Club for Growth's memo is urging Republicans to point to the rapid federal expansion the Biden administration presided over during the COVID-19 pandemic. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE The materials, a two-page memo for lawmakers and a more in-depth 76-page policy packet, also urge Republicans to push policies that Club for Growth says will actually lower those costs. AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING The strategy would be a gamble, given the midterms are traditionally a referendum on how people feel about how they are doing under the party currently in power. But it gives Republicans a potential economic platform and a roadmap to pitch for lowering costs if they keep the majority for the next two years. "The free-market answer is structural cost relief: spend less, build more, produce more energy, make healthcare compete, let workers earn, and let families choose," the memo said. BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT It urged Republicans to resist calling for subsidies for areas of the economy where prices are skyrocketing, arguing that handing out taxpayer money would only increase costs in the longer-term. An example the memo used is Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits, which Republicans have long blamed for skyrocketing healthcare costs before the COVID-era subsidy expired at the beginning of this year. "Subsidies and regulation function as a back door for government control and involvement in private industry," the memo argued. "The only way to address the affordability crisis properly is to undo misguided government intervention and stop pretending more of the same will suddenly work." But it could put GOP lawmakers at odds with President Donald Trump and his promise to give each American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. Several GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital last week were hesitant to embrace the idea. Among the solutions offered are reforming Social Security, which fiscal hawks have long warned will soon run out of cash if changes are not made to current age requirements and other guidelines. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' On high housing costs, the memo urges lawmakers to increase supply by targeting land use and building regulations rather than offering subsidies to make existing housing more affordable. Energy costs, which were a flashpoint in the 2025 off-year elections as well, could be brought down by furthering the Trump administration's goals to unleash U.S. energy sources rather than Democrats' push for net-zero carbon emissions, the memo said. A focus on nuclear energy policies could also help drive down energy costs, which will be at the forefront of most Americans' minds during the November election. And while Democrats have pushed free early childcare as a solution for struggling families, the Club for Growth memo is urging Republicans to find a more lasting solution in reforming regulations surrounding the industry. "Health and safety training in specific areas, adherence to building, fire, and health codes, and comprehensive background checks, including fingerprinting, are reasonable," the memo said. "However, strict and complex rules about work-child ratios, rigid staffing mandates, and regulations on facility specifications, including equipment requirements and zoning classifications, increase operating costs without demonstrable improvements in child wellbeing."
