articles.title: Frontline NATO ally shares shocking take on Russian invasion threat
articles.summary: Estonia's foreign minister tells Fox News Digital that intelligence sees no Russian buildup for a NATO invasion despite rising hybrid attack fears.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Fears that Russia is preparing for a broader war with NATO aren't rattling Estonia's foreign minister, who told Fox News Digital that his country’s intelligence sees no signs Moscow is preparing for a full-scale invasion of the alliance. "We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York City before quipping, "But we don’t see it." Estonia shares a roughly 180-mile border with Russia and has long been among NATO’s most vocal members warning about the threat from Moscow under President Vladimir Putin. But Tsahkna drew a distinction between preparations for a conventional attack and the growing campaign of drone incursions, sabotage, cyberattacks and other provocations that European governments have blamed on Russia. BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT "Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change," Tsahkna said. "We don’t see that Russia is preparing a full-scale invasion or aggression. The other side of our borders is pretty empty." Tsahkna, who served as Estonia’s defense minister from 2016 to 2017, contrasted the current picture with what he saw a decade ago, when he said roughly 120,000 Russian troops were positioned across the region’s borders and could be ready to move within 48 hours. "It’s empty," he said of the Russian side of Estonia’s border today. His assessment comes as European officials grapple with a series of Russian airspace violations and suspected hybrid attacks, including a Russian military helicopter that crossed into Polish airspace Wednesday. Poland’s military said the incursion appeared to be another attempt to test the readiness of its air defenses. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT European and NATO officials have also warned that Russia could rebuild sufficient military capability to pose a direct threat to the alliance in the coming years. Estonia’s own intelligence service said earlier this year that it saw no Russian intention to attack a NATO member in the immediate term, while warning that Moscow’s military reforms are increasing its longer-term capabilities. Tsahkna argued that the more immediate threat is a Russian campaign of provocations and hybrid attacks designed to remain below NATO’s Article 5 threshold. "What Russia is doing now is waging these attacks, which are not crossing Article 5," he said. "It’s sabotage attacks, terror attacks." "The main purpose for Putin is to play with the Western part of the fear of escalation," Tsahkna went on. "He’s trying to divide the Western parts of the world. Divide the unity, divide this kind of consensus." Estonia has dealt with GPS interference, cyberattacks and disinformation it has attributed to Russia, while drones have also crossed into its airspace as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues. Tsahkna said Estonia recorded roughly 40,000 cyberattacks last year, a particular challenge for a country where virtually all public services are available online. "We are witnessing already, yes, any kind of different level attacks," he said. "Unfortunately, it’s already like normality." Tsahkna said NATO needs to become more flexible in responding to attacks that fall below the alliance’s collective-defense threshold. "NATO must be more flex and more dynamic, because these are the attacks which are not crossing Article 5," he said, pointing to sanctions, public attribution and political responses as tools available to the alliance. "Putin wants to boil Europe and Western part of the world as a frog," Tsahkna said. "Turning on the heat piece by piece is a test of us." Tsahkna also pointed to an incident last year in which three Russian fighter jets violated Estonian airspace for roughly 12 minutes, prompting Tallinn to request consultations under NATO’s Article 4 and raise the incident at the U.N. Security Council. He recalled President Donald Trump later saying Russian aircraft that violate NATO airspace should be shot down, and said Estonia has not experienced another comparable fighter-jet incursion since. "We have now drones coming in," Tsahkna said. "NATO is working as a Swiss clock." Tsahkna said NATO may need cheaper and more efficient ways to bring down drones rather than relying on expensive fighter aircraft. On Ukraine, Tsahkna called for increasing pressure on Moscow, arguing that Russia’s economic and battlefield losses could eventually push Putin toward serious negotiations. "What we see, and I also visited Ukraine last week, is that we need to put more pressure on Russia, because Putin understands only very clear language through strength," he said. Tsahkna also pointed to Ukraine’s growing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia as a source of pressure on the Kremlin. "If Putin is under heavier pressure, and also Ukraine is delivering more deep-strike capabilities and attacks, there will be a momentum when Putin may really start some kind of ceasefire or energy ceasefire, or real talks," he said. Tsahkna said Trump had devoted significant effort to seeking an end to the war, but argued that Putin has used the diplomatic process to buy time. "President Trump has put lots of energy during the last year to find a way, but Putin has just played with him and also winning the time," Tsahkna said. He said Ukraine’s deep strikes are already weakening Russia economically, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly signaled his willingness to agree to a ceasefire. "Putin can just decide like today or tomorrow to have a ceasefire," Tsahkna said. "Unfortunately, we don’t see any change for now." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tsahkna also said Estonia has been assured that U.S. forces will remain in the region for the next rotation, amid the Trump administration’s broader review of the American military footprint in Europe. "We got the information that it will happen soon," he said of the next rotation. Tsahkna said the presence of American forces remains an important part of deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank. "U.S. troops are keeping the peace in our region," Tsahkna said. "The flag of the troops is so important to give the message to President Putin" about the red lines between Russia and NATO.

articles.title: Xi caps Trump state visit with symbolic final stop before leaving Washington
articles.summary: Trump and Xi Jinping cap their United States summit with a National Archives visit to view historic documents before the Chinese leader departs.
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping, leader of the country’s ruling Communist Party, will depart the United States today, but not before a final stop at the National Archives. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump will first meet President Xi Jinping and his wife, Madame Peng Liyuan, for morning tea at the White House's Red Room. After that, the couples will head to the National Archives for what the White House describes as a viewing of "a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history." From there, Trump will bid Xi farewell, and the whirlwind two-and-a-half day summit, underscored by a palpable tension, will conclude. The National Archives houses some of America's most important documents, including the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights and the Declaration of Independence. TRUMP-XI SUMMIT SHOULD MAKE SURE AMERICAN STRENGTH DELIVERS AMERICAN RESULTS The two heads of state met at the White House on Thursday morning, which began with a state arrival ceremony consisting of military honors, a review of troops, the Chinese and American national anthems and a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber in formation with four fighter jets. A frenzied press, foreign and domestic, scurried around the White House grounds to catch glimpses of Trump and Xi, who does not often visit the West. Trump and his administration officials held bilateral talks with the Chinese delegation from the late morning into the early afternoon, lasting for several hours. Xi and Trump also spoke behind closed doors in the Oval Office. After the meetings, Trump escorted Xi to the White House's South Lawn, where the pair viewed Marine One, and the new helipad on which it sits. They also toured the White House ballroom, which is under construction, and Trump showed Xi the Presidential Walk of Fame outside the West Wing, which features headshots of presidents past. Trump installed an image of an autopen in Biden’s place on the Presidential Walk of Fame, a reference to Trump’s repeated attacks on the former president’s use of an autopen while in office. Xi and Trump could both be seen laughing at the image, according to footage on social media. Outside the White House gates, protesters against Chinese oppression could be heard chanting throughout the day of meetings. The protests carried into the evening, with chants of "Free Hong Kong," "Xi Jinping, you’re not welcome" and "freedom for political prisoners" at times drowning out the state dinner at the White House, Fox News Digital reported. XI CAN’T ESCAPE PROTESTERS’ CRIES AT DEAFENING DINNER DEMONSTRATION A White House official told Fox News Digital before the visit that Trump would explore a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods in the meeting with Xi. That official also said the nation's leaders would discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls, and that Trump was expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports. Trump called the meeting "great," but didn't elaborate and didn't take questions from the press during the day. China will send two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, to Zoo Atlanta under a conservation agreement, Xi announced. Xi also invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study over the next five years. Xi departed the White House for several hours after the meeting, but returned for a state dinner that officially began at 8:00 p.m. Trump kicked off the dinner with a toast to peace and prosperity for both nations. Guests at the dinner included the second family, Cabinet officials and their spouses, and titans of industry in banking and tech. XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) head Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook were all in attendance. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The inclusion of American artificial intelligence leaders was notable, given that the powerful technology was a hotbed summit issue as China and the United States race for AI dominance.

articles.title: 'Castro's playbook': Ex-AG warns dozens of congressional bills are pushing socialist ideas
articles.summary: Conservative free-market group flags 32 Capitol Hill bills proposing socialist policies "straight from Castro's playbook," as concerns mount over how radical mainstream Democrats are becoming.
articles.body: Federal guarantees for jobs and housing, the elimination of private health insurance, a massive Green New Deal expansion, and new taxes on unrealized wealth are among dozens of current congressional proposals being called out by a national free-market group led by former Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares. Miyares, whose family fled Fidel Castro's communist regime, described the proposed laws seen on Capitol Hill as "straight from Castro’s playbook" in a sit-down interview with Fox News Digital. Miyares recently became the honorary chairman at the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce, a conservative trade organization representing American businesses, which just launched a "Socialism Watch" initiative tracking 32 bills that have been introduced on Capitol Hill aiming to implement what the group describes as socialist policy goals across healthcare, energy, labor, housing, taxation and more. "The year Fidel Castro took power in Cuba, Cuba had the same GDP as Greece. The year that he died, too bad the same GDP as Sudan," Miyares told Fox News Digital. "Socialism doesn't work. It impoverishes every country that embraces it." DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT Among the bills highlighted by Miyares and the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce is legislation that would ban fracking nationwide beginning in 2029, prohibit greenhouse-gas emissions from power plants and restrict new liquefied natural gas infrastructure and most U.S. oil and natural gas exports. Others would create government-backed job-guarantee programs offering employment to qualifying applicants, replace private health insurance with a national Medicare for All program and impose annual taxes on accumulated wealth, even when those gains have not been realized through a sale. The group is also zeroing in on a massive progressive push to overhaul American real estate: the "Housing is a Human Right Act." While supporters pitch the $300 billion bill as a moral crusade to end homelessness, critics like Miyares see it differently. They argue that by officially declaring shelter a government-guaranteed right and pumping billions into "social housing," the legislation is actively trying to push private landlords out of the market. TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS Other measures flagged by the group include a proposal to create a quasi-governmental "National Infrastructure Bank" to fund politically favored state projects, alongside a $1.6 trillion "Green New Deal for Public Schools" that the American Free Enterprise Chamber of Commerce warns would hand local school district operations over to the federal government. "These young people are embracing socialism thinking that it leads to helping those that are poor, disadvantaged. The reality is it does the opposite," Miyares told Fox News Digital. "It actually hurts the very people that it wants to help." Miyares' warnings about socialism are rooted in his family's history in Cuba. His mother, Miriam, fled Fidel Castro's communist regime in 1965 at 19 years old, arriving in the United States after leaving nearly everything behind. Miyares has said his uncle, an opponent of Castro, was arrested following the Bay of Pigs invasion and subjected to a mock execution, an experience he has said helped drive his mother's decision to leave the island. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "So many young people have forgotten really, really painful lessons of history that you cannot judge a bill or an economic system based on intentions, you have to judge it on results," Miyares said. "What we've seen time and time again is socialism fails everywhere it's been tried." But Miyares argued the debate is no longer confined to activists or ideological arguments outside Washington, pointing to the 32 bills tracked through the American Free Enterprise Chamber’s newly launched "Socialism Watch" initiative as evidence that policies associated with the socialist-left have made their way into actual legislation before Congress. "AOC joked that woke one was crazy," Miyares said. "Well, it’s clear that woke two should belong in an insane asylum because it’s a full-blown embrace of Marxism and socialism."

articles.title: Bill Gates says AI companies self-regulating isn’t enough and governments should be involved in monitoring
articles.summary: Bill Gates called for lawmakers in Washington to regulate the development of artificial intelligence, weeks after the CEOs of some of the nation’s biggest AI labs agreed on the need to slow the pace of AI progress.
articles.body: Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates on Wednesday called for lawmakers in Washington to regulate the development of artificial intelligence, weeks after the CEOs of some of the nation’s biggest AI labs agreed on the need to slow the pace of AI progress. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” Gates told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” in an interview set to air in full Sunday. Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether there needs to be legislation passed in Washington, Gates said, “Absolutely.” “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” he said. “And that has to be a required thing. And it will be a little bit of overhead for the industry, but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.” Earlier this month, the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI, two of the nation’s biggest AI labs, agreed that the race to develop powerful AI systems should slow down. Their statements on the issue came after a whistleblower who recently resigned from Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, publicly declared that “neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon added in a series of social media posts and interviews that week. In Wednesday’s interview, Gates didn’t downplay the risk that AI could wipe out humanity in several years, but called for Americans not to ignore the risks that AI could be used by bad actors to cause large-scale harm as soon as today. “AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths. You know, so even though it’s pretty hard to get to 100%, there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” he said. In an interview with “Meet the Press” earlier this month, Coxon said that AI companies should be allowed to regulate themselves. “I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” he said. Appearing earlier on the same program several weeks ago, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., declined to bring House lawmakers back to Washington to pass legislation to regulate the pace of AI growth, saying that he would defer to the AI companies. “We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” the speaker said, adding that while AI CEOs had called for a slowdown, they hadn’t yet offered a path forward that involved federal legislation. “They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” Johnson said. In his essay calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei specifically called for global and federal cooperation. “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all U.S. frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” he wrote, adding later in the piece: “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities.” Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, on Wednesday spoke before a gathering of the United Nations, calling for international standards for “measuring capabilities, assessing risks, determining whether safeguards are sufficient and preserving meaningful human oversight” over AI. Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg disagreed with that approach. “I don’t think that we need some kind of industrywide coordination,” he told NBC News in an interview published Thursday. “I think that each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to basically make sure that you’re proceeding safely.” At the state level, some governors have already begun the process of regulating AI companies and the data centers they use to power their development. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom last week signed an executive order creating a board of experts tasked with creating a plan for the state to strengthen its laws on AI safety. This week, in Maryland and New York, Govs. Wes Moore and Kathy Hochul each also released plans aimed at boosting AI regulation in their states. Moore’s order creates a “three pronged approach” to regulation, while Hochul’s creates a new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust to oversee legal compliance for AI companies. Speaking at a United Nations session on AI and human development this week, Microsoft President Brad Smith rejected the notion that AI companies have to wait for federal regulation to slow themselves down and criticized them for constantly racing against each other to make more advanced AI products. “Imagine for a moment that there’s only two big companies in the world that produce commercial airplanes,” Smith said. “Imagine that somebody comes into your office and says, ‘I know we’re in a race to get out the next airplane first, but we’re worried that the airplane will crash and people will die.’ Would you say, ‘I need to win this race’?” Smith asked. “Or, would you say, ‘I’m going to put the safety of my passengers and the safety of the public ahead of my winning that race’? That is the fundamental question.”

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel touts what separates himself from other Dems as he mulls 2028 presidential bid
articles.summary: In an interview with Fox News Digital, former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel spoke about what separates himself from other Democrats as he mulls a 2028 bid.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — Former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel hasn't been shy about his potential prospects for the White House, but as 2028 approaches, the hypothetical Democratic field continues to get more crowded. In an interview with Fox News Digital at the Texas Tribune Festival, Emanuel pointed to three things that separate him from the pack — if he chooses to run. "Candor, authenticity and strength," Emanuel told Fox News Digital. RAHM EMANUEL SPARS WITH NEW YORKER INTERVIEWER WHO GRILLED HIM FOR NOT EMPHASIZING TRANS ISSUES Emanuel's resume in Democratic politics is quite extensive, from serving as a top advisor for Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, to a congressman, to the mayor of Chicago to, more recently, serving as America's top diplomat in Japan under the Biden administration. If elected president, he insists he "knows what to do on day one." "I'm not gonna tell you what you'd like to hear. I'm gonna tell you what you need to know to make some of the tough decisions ahead," Emanuel said. "We don't have time anymore. We're at a tipping point in the country. I think we've wasted a lot of time in the last 12 years trying to restore, as I said, a past that's not coming back. We better think about a future that includes everybody. We don't have a person to waste or a community to overlook and make the investments that make this country stronger." "And so I'm gonna be honest about it. And I think I bring a level of experience at multiple levels of government that actually, on day one, you start getting the job done. Because we don't have a day to waste," he added. RAHM EMANUEL SLAMS DNC AUTOPSY AND JILL BIDEN, SAYING PARTY NOW LOOKS 'WORSE THAN FECKLESS' The former ambassador has a long road ahead of him to seek the Democratic nomination as the RealClearPolitics average of polls currently does not have him among the top 10 contenders. articles.title: El Ayuntamiento de Lleida prohíbe el burka o el niqab en los espacios públicos
articles.standfirst: El artículo 12 de la ordenanza, que es el que regula dicha prohibición, contempla sanciones de entre 400 y 750 euros por el incumplimiento de la norma
articles.summary: El artículo 12 de la ordenanza, que es el que regula dicha prohibición, contempla sanciones de entre 400 y 750 euros por el incumplimiento de la norma
articles.body: El Ayuntamiento de Lleida ha aprobado este viernes la ordenanza municipal por la que prohíbe llevar en los espacios públicos elementos que "oculten totalmente el rostro", como el burka o el niqab, eso sí sin mención expresa a estas prendas, detalla EFE. Dicha nueva ordenanza, que se fundamenta en el civismo y el derecho de las mujeres y no en la seguridad, ha contado con los nueve votos a favor del PSC-Units (en el Gobierno), de los cinco concejales de Junts y de los dos de Vox, mientras que PP, ERC y el Comú han votado en contra. Al respecto de ello, el artículo 12 de la ordenanza, que es el que regula la prohibición del burka, contempla sanciones de entre 400 y 750 euros por el incumplimiento de la norma, que no se aplicará en los lugares de culto ni en los espacios donde sea habitual ir con el rostro cubierto en atención a las costumbres sociales aceptadas o cuando se haga en el ejercicio de un derecho fundamental. En febrero del año 2013, el Tribunal Supremo ya anuló una ordenanza municipal en Lleida que prohibió el uso del velo integral en los espacios municipales. Por aquel entonces, el alto tribunal argumentó en su sentencia que un consistorio no puede limitar un derecho fundamental como el de la libertad religiosa. En febrero de este mismo año, el Congreso rechazó la propuesta de Vox, apoyada por el PP, para prohibir el burka, mientras que Junts presentó su propia ley.

articles.title: Liberal justice hammers Supreme Court for fast-tracking emergency docket cases
articles.summary: Ketanji Brown Jackson slammed the Supreme Court's emergency docket, warning it gives certain litigants a "fast pass" that undermines standard review.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson ripped her colleagues for fast-tracking cases on the high court’s emergency docket, saying "it has been noticeably less restrained, especially with respect to pending cases that involve controversial matters." The emergency docket, sometimes known as the shadow or interim docket, allows parties to ask the Supreme Court to quickly intervene in lawsuits and temporarily pause lower court rulings. The process can take a couple of days, weeks or months, and is viewed as a much speedier, although temporary, way to secure court relief than when the court fully considers the merits of a case, which can include a long briefing schedule and oral arguments. "Why is it that one party should get a fast pass to the Supreme Court of the United States, when so many other parties are queued up, waiting patiently for the court’s attention?" Jackson said Thursday during a speech at the University of the District of Columbia’s law school, according to The Hill. "If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end run around the standard review process, a special avenue that certain privileged litigants can use selectively," she added. SUPREME COURT DECLINES TO INTERVENE IN CASE OF SURROGATE MOTHER WHO REFUSED ABORTION Jackson's speech comes as the Trump administration has submitted 40 emergency applications to the Supreme Court since the start of the president's second term, The Hill reported. Through the emergency docket, the Supreme Court has greenlit Trump's mass firings of career employees and high-profile terminations of Democratic appointees. It has curtailed nationwide injunctions and cleared the way for controversial deportations and immigration stops. Since the start of Trump’s second term, his administration has won about 80% of its appeals on the emergency docket, according to Politico. KAVANAUGH THROWS TRUMP 'A LIFELINE' ON MAIL BALLOT RULES DESPITE SUPREME COURT LOSS BEFORE MIDTERMS The Supreme Court’s majority has often split along ideological lines and offered little reason for its emergency decisions. This differs from final orders from the court, which can be lengthy and include numerous concurring opinions and dissents. Jackson also said Thursday that parties should be required to prove impending harm in cases that cannot wait for full adjudication by the lower courts, as opposed to the Supreme Court granting stay applications based on whether lower courts could have made mistakes, Courthouse News Service reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Significant real-world harms can follow Supreme Court stay rulings, and when the court’s orders do not acknowledge that reality, they seem oblivious and ring hollow," Jackson was quoted as saying. "We cannot expect the public to have faith in our judicial system if, without clear explanation, we are consistently greenlighting harmful acts that do real damage to litigating plaintiffs without a court decision fully and fairly determining the lawfulness of that challenged conduct on the merits." Fox News Digital’s Ashley Oliver contributed to this report.

articles.title: U.S. military lays groundwork for potential action around Cuba
articles.summary: Some units would "possibly [be] needed in 90-120 days," according to an internal Army message reviewed by CBS News.
articles.body:
Washington — The U.S. Army Reserve is examining whether it can provide the military's Southern Command with police forces, medical personnel and other support units within the next four months, according to an internal Army message reviewed by CBS News.

Though the message makes no reference to Cuba, the request is for continued military planning aimed at Cuba, according to multiple U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

There is no indication in the document that any units have received deployment orders. But the planning comes as the Trump administration puts intense economic pressure on Cuba and urges the island nation to make political reforms.

The message does not identify how many troops would be needed in the Southern Command's region, which covers Central and South America, including the Caribbean. It also does not specify where the forces could be sent or what operation they would support.

The document reviewed by CBS News says Army Reserve headquarters is seeking feedback from subordinate commands on the possible availability of six types of formations that would fall under the authority of U.S. Southern Command. The units would "possibly [be] needed in 90-120 days," according to the message, which directs commands to provide feedback to Army Reserve headquarters by Sept. 25.

Among the units is a combat sustainment support battalion that specializes in coordinating logistics such as transportation, maintenance, fuel and supply needs, along with an engineer battalion. The document also seeks an expeditionary sustainment command that would oversee logistics across a theater of operations.

The document generated last week also calls for a medical brigade to command and coordinate medical units, as well as a forward resuscitative and surgical detachment to provide emergency surgery and trauma care closer to U.S. forces. Finally, the document seeks a military police brigade — these units typically oversee military police forces responsible for security, detention and other law enforcement missions.

Contacted by CBS News, the Army Reserve did not respond before publication.

A spokesperson for U.S. Southern Command said: "Due to operational security concerns, we do not disclose details or comment on U.S. operational movements or potential deployment timelines associated with current or future operations, contingencies, or planning. However, U.S. Southern Command continuously coordinates with the Joint Force to assess a range of potential requirements across its [area of responsibility] in support of assigned missions."

Earlier this year, American forces conducted reconnaissance operations on the seafloor and maritime approaches surrounding the Cuban island, multiple U.S. military personnel told CBS News. Separately, U.S. airpower components were placed on heightened readiness and directed to pre-stage personnel for potential deployment. Those plans, however, did not come to fruition. CBS News is withholding certain details from publication that could potentially put U.S. service members at risk.

CBS News reported in May that U.S. intelligence officials were assessing how Cuba would respond to possible U.S. military action, as the Trump administration accused Havana of strengthening ties with Russia, China and Iran. The intelligence community's 2026 annual threat assessment largely portrays Cuba as an enabling environment for larger geopolitical competitors, rather than as an independent strategic threat.

In July, CBS News reported that American military planners had examined a range of options for possible action against the island, including an Army-led air assault involving thousands of U.S. soldiers to be carried out by the 101st Airborne Division, the only unit trained for such a task.

U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News stressed in July that the briefings were not an indication that the president or the Pentagon had decided to go forward with an operation.

Since reentering office, President Trump has asserted a more muscular U.S. role in the Western Hemisphere under what officials have dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine," a Trump-era corollary to the Monroe Doctrine focused on limiting foreign adversaries and other perceived threats in the region.

In April, American and Ecuadorian troops launched a joint mission aimed at dismantling a suspected criminal hub operated by a narco-terrorist organization. On Thursday, U.S. troops and agents with the Drug Enforcement Administration assisted Ecuadorian authorities in arresting more than 30 members affiliated with Mexico's Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

Since September, the U.S. military has killed more than 230 people in 70 strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean. The operations are a stark contrast from the U.S. military's historical role of maritime drug interdiction and arrest. Some legal experts have said the strikes amount to illegal extrajudicial killings because U.S. forces are prohibited from intentionally targeting civilians or individuals suspected of criminal activity, unless they meet the legal standard governing the use of military force.

For Cuba, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Cuban entities and officials, including military research and development enterprises tied to the country's nickel industry ahead of the U.N. General Assembly this week.

In New York, Mr. Trump told the U.N. General Assembly that his administration was seeking a "fundamental change" on the island and predicted Cuba's communist government "will fall" and declared that "freedom will be coming to Cuba." The Cuban delegation walked out during his remarks.

Mr. Trump also said Secretary of State Marco Rubio was "deep into negotiations" with Havana and vowed that the United States would not allow foreign adversaries to establish a strengthening foothold "on our own doorstep."

Those remarks follow months of increasingly explicit statements from Mr. Trump about Cuba. Meanwhile, Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel has vowed to counter any U.S. attack , and has accused the U.S. of "aggression" and "economic warfare" by blocking oil imports to Cuba.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed he would have "the honor of taking Cuba."

"Taking Cuba in some form, yeah," he said in mid-March. "Taking Cuba. I mean, whether I free it, take it — I think I could do anything I want with it, if you want to know the truth."

Later that month, Mr. Trump said bluntly: "Cuba's going to be next."

articles.title: Trump revives Supreme Court immigration showdown after Hochul pardon torpedoed first case
articles.summary: The Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to decide whether criminal aliens in ICE detention are entitled to bond hearings during removal.
articles.body: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to revive a major immigration fight over whether criminal aliens can be held without bond throughout removal proceedings or are entitled to a hearing when their detention drags on. Solicitor General John Sauer asked the Supreme Court on Monday to take up Genalo v. D.C., reviving a constitutional fight the justices had been set to hear this term in Genalo v. Black before New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul’s pardon rendered that case moot. At the center of the dispute is D.C., a Dominican national who is facing removal after a criminal history that includes drug trafficking and domestic violence charges. He had previously been removed from the United States on six occasions, according to ICE. Federal law requires certain criminal aliens to remain in custody while their deportation cases play out. But the Second Circuit has ruled that if they are detained for too long, they are entitled to a bond hearing at which the government must make the case for keeping them in custody. BLUE STATE GOVERNOR'S PARDON OF CONVICTED FELON TORPEDOS A MAJOR SUPREME COURT IMMIGRATION FIGHT Other appeals courts have taken different approaches, leaving the Supreme Court with a nationwide split over what constitutional protections apply. "So the rights of these criminal aliens who were being detained, whether or not they're entitled to a bond hearing as of right now depends on which jurisdiction they happen to fall in," Michael Morley, a Florida State University law professor, told Fox News Digital. "And so the government is asking the Supreme Court to set one uniform interpretation for the entire country." The Trump administration's petition is procedurally unusual because Genalo v. D.C. is still pending before the Second Circuit. Sauer is asking the Supreme Court to intervene before the appeals court issues its decision. "Rather than making the court go through those motions, you just hear this case now, hear this case directly, even before the Second Circuit has had the opportunity to rule," Morley told Fox News Digital. The legal dispute could also determine who carries the burden when a bond hearing is required. Under the Second Circuit's approach, the government must show that a detainee poses a flight risk or danger to the community. The administration argued that if the Constitution requires such hearings, the burden should instead fall on the detainee seeking release. Lawyers supporting the administration argue that some detainees could delay their removal cases, then use the length of their detention to seek release on bond. "The biggest issue that happens here is gamemanship," Chad Mizelle, chair of litigation at the America First Policy Institute and a former acting associate attorney general, told Fox News Digital. "A lot of times these aliens will file multiple applications for asylum, withholding removal. They'll get new attorneys, switch out attorneys, ask for continuances, ask for delays," Mizelle said. "So all of a sudden they've been in detention now, six, seven, eight months, completely of their own making." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA Mizelle argued that if prolonged detention eventually gives a detainee the right to seek bond, it could create an incentive to stretch proceedings long enough to reach that point. "They would switch out attorneys. They would make frivolous filings regarding asylum, regarding withholding of removal. They would ask for delays and continuances upon delays and continuances," Mizelle said. "They'll do everything they can to try to stretch this out, six months, seven months, eight months, file a habeas petition, say that they're entitled to a bond hearing, and then if they are released, abscond." Carrie Severino, president of the Judicial Crisis Network, similarly described the additional litigation as "a foot dragging, sand in the gears exercise." "This is attempting to stall, attempting to run out the clock or just, you know, the question is whether there even is a clock," Severino told Fox News Digital. She pointed to cases such as Demore v. Kim, in which detainees themselves sought additional time during proceedings before later challenging the length of their detention. OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’ SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "So, it's often a situation where people are playing both sides of it," Severino said. "But they're asking for more time on different things, but then at the same time complaining that the whole process is taking too long." However, Severino cautioned that she could not speak to the motivations of every detainee. The Supreme Court has previously upheld mandatory detention during removal proceedings, but Morley said the High Court has left open the constitutional question now at the center of the administration's petition. "This is a question that the [Supreme Court] itself went out of its way, you can say, to leave open for adjudication in a future case," Morley said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The administration is now asking the justices not to wait for another one. "You wanted to resolve this case. Here's another case that presents the same exact question that lets you resolve the circuit split this term," Morley said. "So basically, substitute this case for the moot case." Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

articles.title: How private equity is killing public access to hospitals and emergency care
articles.summary: The corporatization of the health care system by private equity has come with significant costs. While private equity’s ownership of hospitals may earn millions for their investors, they have put patients, communities and providers at risk.
articles.body:
For more than two decades, I have worked in emergency departments across Chicago, and I have watched what happens when a hospital disappears from a neighborhood that depended upon it.

The ambulances have to drive farther, waiting rooms fill faster, and patients arrive sicker because the care they needed wasn’t there when they needed it. What I didn’t expect over the course of my career was to watch this happen not because a neighborhood couldn’t support the hospital, but because the hospital’s assets may be worth more extracted than operating.

In March 2026, West Suburban Medical Center, located in Oak Park, Ill., became the third hospital in Chicago’s safety net to abruptly close. Weiss Memorial Hospital also closed unexpectedly in 2025, and Westlake Hospital in Melrose Park in 2019. The common denominator is that all three were, at one point, owned by Pipeline Health, a private-equity-backed hospital chain that acquired them in 2019.

This is not just a Chicago story — it is happening all across the country . Approximately 447 hospitals are now under private-equity ownership , and about 25 percent serve rural populations. While private-equity-backed companies generate roughly 7 percent of U.S. GDP, they accounted for 21 percent of all health care bankruptcies in 2024, and seven of the eight largest health care bankruptcies that year.

Most notably, Steward Health Care, once the largest private for-profit hospital system in the country, was purchased by a private-equity firm in 2010 and sold in 2020. Four years later, the hospital system closed both their safety net hospitals and filed for bankruptcy, leaving a vulnerable patient population without access to health care and many miles away from potentially time-sensitive emergency care with prolonged emergency medical transport times.

Safety-net hospitals serve a patient population that is disproportionately low-income, publicly insured and racially and ethnically diverse. According to America’s Essential Hospitals, 75 percent of the patients are either uninsured or covered by Medicaid or Medicare. These hospitals are frequently the sole local source of high-acuity services for rural and urban communities. As the front door to acute care, these hospitals see twice as many emergency department visits on average.

Serving high volumes of low-income patients, most safety-net hospitals rely on targeted public financing to offset uncompensated and under-reimbursed care. The commitment to the mission of providing care for vulnerable populations, as opposed to targeting payer mix, contributes to their financially fragile existence. As a result, the thin-margin, public payer-dependent structure makes safety-net and rural hospitals targets for leveraged buyouts, sale-leasebacks and, unfortunately, closures.

The corporatization of the health care system by private equity has come with significant costs. While private equity’s ownership of hospitals may earn millions for their investors, they have put patients, communities and providers at risk.

A bipartisan U.S. Senate Budget Committee investigation, which reviewed more than a million internal documents, concluded that private-equity firms “extracted huge profits from hospitals, while increasing their debt and allowing patient care and safety to decline,” and that in some cases this directly forced closures.

A 2023 study in the Journal of the America Medical Association found a 25 percent increase in preventable adverse events at hospitals after private-equity acquisition, including a 38 percent rise in central-line bloodstream infections and a doubling of surgical-site infections.

A more recent study in the Annals of Internal Medicine linked private-equity ownership to cuts in staffing and a corresponding 13 percent increase in emergency room deaths.

And a July 2024 study found that hospital assets fell by 24 percent , on average, in the two years after a private-equity purchase, approximately $28 million per hospital in buildings, equipment and infrastructure that simply disappeared.

None of this is inevitable. It is the predictable result of a specific financing model, and policymakers are beginning to treat it that way. Lawmakers in 25 states, including Illinois, have introduced at least 79 bills, and enacted several addressing private-equity ownership of medical facilities.

And this is happening as a much larger threat looms. Federal Medicaid restructuring passed in 2025 is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by roughly $1 trillion over the next decade, with new provisions set to hit Illinois starting in January 2027.

Safety-net hospitals, which by definition serve the highest share of Medicaid patients, will absorb the brunt of that reduction. It is worth asking what happens to the remaining safety-net hospitals once their primary funding source shrinks even further.

Safety-net hospitals are not distressed assets waiting to be flipped. Instead, they often may be the difference between a stroke caught in time and one that isn’t, between a gunshot wound stabilized in minutes and one that isn’t, between a neighborhood that can care for its own and one that has to drive a considerable distance to do so.

Private-equity groups promise efficiency and turnaround, but as a physician, health care advocate and concerned citizen committed to health and well-being for all, the million-dollar question remains “Efficient for whom?”

Heather Prendergast, MD, is a professor of emergency medicine, attending physician, and vice dean of clinical affairs at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, and a Public Voices Fellow of the OpED Project at the University of Illinois.

articles.title: New Jersey governor calls on lieutenant governor to resign over ethics report
articles.summary: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell (D) until Friday to resign over a new ethics report that found he violated state policy against discrimination in the workplace. Investigators with a law firm hired by Sherrill’s office found Caldwell twice attempted to get his girlfriend promoted to a state role, made…
articles.body:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell (D) until Friday to resign over a new ethics report that found he violated state policy against discrimination in the workplace.

Investigators with a law firm hired by Sherrill’s office found Caldwell twice attempted to get his girlfriend promoted to a state role, made a sexually charged comment to a staff member and did not heed warnings to change his behavior.

The governor said in a statement the investigation found the lieutenant governor “engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office.”

“I hold everyone in my Administration to the highest ethical standard,” she continued. “We all have a duty to follow our state ethics and harassment policy and our Code of Conduct. Anyone who violates these will be held accountable.”

Sherrill said it was “necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents” for him to step down.

“The President continues to undermine confidence in public service at the federal level,” she added. “In New Jersey, I will not accept a culture that sweeps misconduct under the rug. We have to be better than that — people expect and deserve better.”

In one instance included in the report, investigators said Caldwell “made a romantic advance” toward the female friend of one of his staffers. When this advance was rejected, he reportedly told the staffer, “You young women are looking for young sperm.”

Investigators said Caldwell denied making this comment, but they “did not find his denial credible.”

In another instance, investigators found Caldwell recommended his romantic partner for a “senior leadership position” during an ongoing ethics investigation into his behavior. The woman was not ultimately awarded a promotion or benefit after state officials pressed Caldwell about their relationship.

In a statement provided to The New York Times , Caldwell’s attorney, Thomas Calcagni, criticized the investigation as one-sided and said it “lacked the requisite due process.”

The Hill has reached out to Calcagni about whether his client will heed the governor’s call to resign.

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) supported Sherrill’s statement and called the findings in the ethics report “totally unacceptable” in a post online .

“For the sake of our state Lt Governor Caldwell should resign,” he wrote on the social platform X.

articles.title: Trump mourns death of man shot at Butler rally: ‘Tremendous loss’
articles.summary: President Trump mourned the loss of Jim Copenhaver, the man who was shot and injured during the attempted assassination of Trump in Butler, Pa., in 2024. Copenhaver died earlier this week. He was 76. He was one of the two attendees who were shot at the rally where a bullet grazed Trump’s ear. Copenhaver was struck…
articles.body:
President Trump mourned the loss of Jim Copenhaver, the man who was shot and injured during the attempted assassination of Trump in Butler, Pa., in 2024.

Copenhaver died earlier this week. He was 76. He was one of the two attendees who were shot at the rally where a bullet grazed Trump’s ear. Copenhaver was struck by two bullets in his arm and abdomen, leaving him with nerve damage.

“God bless American Patriot and Warrior, James Copenhaver, and his incredible family. May he rest in peace!!!” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

He called Copenhaver a “true American patriot” in a post Thursday, saying his death is a “tremendous loss.”

“More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice,” Trump wrote.

“After being wounded while protecting his family, Jim showed tremendous bravery, courageously continuing to FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT, and maintaining a positive spirit despite unimaginable hardships,” he continued. “His indelible legacy of love and devotion will forever endure. Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne. God bless you all!”

His death was first announced by the House Republican Conference on Thursday.

“We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jim Copenhaver, who was gravely wounded in the horrific shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania,” the conference posted on social media.

Several Republican lawmakers also responded to the news of Copenhaver’s death.

“My prayers are with the family members of Jim Copenhaver, as they grieve his loss,” Arizona Rep. Andy Biggs (R) wrote in a post . “His passing should serve as continued motivation to provide sufficient answers and closure for the investigation into the attempted assassination of President Trump in Butler, where two innocent lives have now been lost.”

articles.title: Chinese media scuffle with US journalists, Secret Service during Xi visit
articles.summary: Members of the Chinese press corps traveling with President Xi Jinping scuffled with U.S. journalists and Secret Service personnel at the White House on Thursday as reporters scrambled to cover the Chinese leader’s state visit. Videos posted online showed several confrontations throughout the day, including Chinese journalists arguing with White House staff and Secret Service…
articles.body:
Members of the Chinese press corps traveling with President Xi Jinping scuffled with U.S. journalists and Secret Service personnel at the White House on Thursday as reporters scrambled to cover the Chinese leader’s state visit.

Videos posted online showed several confrontations throughout the day, including Chinese journalists arguing with White House staff and Secret Service agents over where they could stand during Xi’s arrival ceremony and military review in the Rose Garden.

One video showed journalists packed together as they competed for space ahead of Xi’s arrival. An American journalist could be heard saying, “You’re stepping on my feet.”

Another dispute broke out on the South Lawn over the positioning of U.S. outlets and Chinese state media.

Washington Examiner White House correspondent Christian Datoc said Secret Service and White House officials threatened to remove a Chinese official who was interfering with official White House camera positions.

Video from the scene showed agents attempting to move members of the Chinese press as voices were raised.

Tensions continued inside the White House, where a Chinese photographer reportedly shoved a female American reporter in a packed briefing room as journalists rushed to cover President Trump and Xi’s meeting in the Oval Office.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth also reportedly reacted to a disruption created by the Chinese press corps in the Grand Foyer of the White House, according to Daily Wire White House correspondent Mary Margaret Olohan, who described the visiting press corps as “incredibly loud and aggressive.”

Trump reportedly joked that China had the friendliest press corps.

The confrontations unfolded during a chaotic day for the White House press corps.

Journalists from major television networks ABC, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News were present at the White House but continued withholding their participation in the television pool until they received confirmation that CNN, MS NOW and Politico had regained access to the complex.

The three outlets, barred from the White House by Trump last week, were allowed back in around midday Thursday after a federal judge ordered the White House to restore their access, following a court hearing Wednesday.

Still, some CNN and MS NOW reporters were blocked from covering the state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening.

articles.title: 'Red carpet for a despot': Trump's lavish Xi welcome collides with GOP anti-communism message
articles.summary: Republican senators criticized President Donald Trump's lavish Washington summit with Xi Jinping, warning against red carpet treatment for China's leader.
articles.body: As President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping comes to its end, some Republicans aren’t happy with the red carpet treatment the face of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) received. "Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America, based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party," Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said. Wicker, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, has been one of the more vocal Republicans about his disdain for the meeting, which kicked off Wednesday afternoon when Trump met Xi at Joint Base Andrews — the first time a president has met with a foreign dignitary there since 2015. BIPARTISAN DUO WANTS TO REMIND CONGRESS, TRUMP OF CHINA'S 'ATROCITIES' AHEAD OF XI VISIT The White House argued in a statement to Fox News Digital that Trump was returning the sentiment to Jinping after his visit to Beijing earlier this year. "President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said. "The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people." It comes as Republicans are running to hold onto power in the Senate. They departed their midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month with a rallying cry: "Common sense versus communism," as progressive candidates surge across the country. The convention was designed to remind voters that while his name is not on the ballot, Trump’s agenda is. But his meeting with Xi, optically, runs afoul of that. "I mean, the president campaigned on an anti-China policy," Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. "You go look at those MAGA rallies and look at everybody cheering when he said he's gonna take it to China." "Any time we roll out the red carpet for a despot from Russia, or a despot from China, I feel the same way," he continued. "It's kind of not good." GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’ Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, said he was not "enthusiastic" about the summit, and said that China, Russia, Iran and North Korea were an "axis opposed" to the U.S. "I hope the president's clear-eyed about who he's dealing with," Cornyn told Fox News Digital. "I mean, he tends to call some of these dictators friends, and they're no friend. I can guarantee." Some Republicans are willing to accept that a meeting between Trump and Xi is a necessary step in building a relationship between the two superpowers, even with the lavish nature of the summit. "I think there's value in being able to talk with your adversaries," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital. "And I think, in this case, you know, our two countries, the biggest economies in the world, have a symbiotic relationship." Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., was invited to attend the dinner after spending years working in China before running for office. Daines told Fox News Digital that he understood his colleagues’ apprehension, but that the U.S. and China, and particularly Trump and Xi’s relationship, had to work. TRUMP-XI SUMMIT COULD HOLD KEY TO LOWER GAS PRICES, GOP CHAIRMAN SAYS "This relationship is too big to fail, and it's only appropriate that President Trump and his team extends respect to Xi Jinping, and it's really reciprocal to what they did for President Trump back in May when they showed him great respect when he showed up in Beijing," Daines said. Still, that doesn’t mean Republicans have to like it. "It is one of his strengths, his ability to sort of win individuals over with hospitality," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told Fox News Digital. "He's in the business. So I don't, again, I'm not gonna second guess it. You know, I hate seeing it at a personal level, but I trust his instincts on it." Lawmakers hoped that the two-and-a-half-day summit would yield deals on the artificial intelligence (AI) race, trade deals that would end the trade war between the U.S. and China and for Xi to use his influence to get oil and natural gas flowing through the Strait of Hormuz again. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump kept tight-lipped about the nature of their bilateral meeting in the Oval Office on Thursday, but so far, Xi has promised two new pandas while the president is mulling allowing Chinese electric vehicles to be built in the U.S. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., took no issue with the meeting, but hoped that Trump would see through any smokescreen Xi deployed. "I just suggested, and I don't think he will — the president's a pretty good judge of character — not to believe President Xi’s bulls---, because he's lying. Particularly about helping Iran, and Xi could get the Strait open immediately if he wanted," Kennedy told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Washington must rejoin the Saudi war against the Houthis
articles.summary: Ceding the region to China surely is not a prospect Washington should relish, even if it wishes to lower its Middle Eastern profile.
articles.body:
The Houthis have been in an intermittent war with Saudi Arabia for a dozen years, but their resentment of Saudi Arabia stretches back nearly a century.

In the 1920s, King Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia seized the Asir province that historically had been under Zaidi Muslim control. When the rulers of Yemen tried to reclaim the territory, they were defeated by the Saudis in 1934. The Houthis, a mountain people, are Zaidis, the Saudis are Wahhabi Sunnis. The Houthis are committed to restoring Zaidi rule, which had ended in 1962, and continue to resent the loss of Asir.

In 2004, the Houthis revolted against the north Yemeni government of Ali Saleh when Saleh sought to arrest their leader, Hussein Badereddin al-Houthi. Al-Houthi died the same year, but the rebellion did not die with him. As the war dragged on, the Saudis intervened on behalf of Saleh’s government.

Ten years after their initial uprising, the Houthis captured Sana’a, the ancient north Yemeni capital. In response, the Saudis, with American intelligence and logistical support, tried but failed to drive back the Houthis. Instead, with Iranian assistance, including arms and trainers, the Houthis continued to expand their control over north Yemeni territory.

After several years of peace, the Houthis intervened on behalf of Hamas in its war with Israel. In 2024 they fired missiles at Israel, prompting Israeli attacks on their formations. They also attacked Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea, expanded those attacks to ships from other countries, and fired missiles and drones on American and British naval units that were defending vessels transiting the Red and Arabian seas.

The attacks continued when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in 2025, and after holding their fire after renewed American operations against Iran in February, the Houthis, with Iranian encouragement, seized key islands in the Bab el Mandeb strait and closed it to Saudi shipping. They also attacked Saudi military and civilian targets, including targeting drones and missiles on Mecca and Riyadh .

The Saudis are receiving support from Pakistan, their Mecca Treaty allies, which has deployed 8,000 troops and air defense systems, and has sent a squadron of Chinese-built J-17 fighter aircraft to the King Abdul Aziz air base. The 600 miles from the base to the Houthi strongholds constitutes the outer limits of the fighters’ combat radius, however. It would be difficult to conduct more than one attack before having to return to base.

In any event, the Pakistanis have thus far not launched any attacks on the Houthis, and their forces are likely to remain in a defensive posture.

Riyadh’s other Mecca Treaty allies, the Turks, have offered to assist the Saudis, but thus far have not committed forces to defend them or attack the Houthis — no doubt because Ankara’s forces continue to operate in Syria and Iraq.

Thanks to Houthi attacks on both Red Sea shipping and Saudi oil pipelines , together with its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has been able to throttle Saudi oil exports. The kingdom is facing the prospect of economic contraction , while finding itself unable to defeat the Houthis, especially as it continues to suffer from Iranian missile attacks.

Riyadh has turned to America for assistance, but thus far the Saudis have been rebuffed . Washington is committed to its operations against Iran and faces an increasing munitions shortfall that would seriously worsen if it again joined the fight against the Houthis, who have threatened to retaliate.

Leaving the Saudis to their own devices will simply encourage Riyadh to reevaluate its relationship with the U.S., however. Its defense strategy has been predicated on America’s rushing to its defense in the event of Iranian attack, yet until now American forces have been unable to prevent Iranian missiles and drones from inflicting extensive damage on Saudi military and civilian targets.

No doubt China, which long has had an excellent economic relationship with the Saudis and in the past has sold them weapons, would act quickly to fill any vacuum that Washington leaves. Should the Saudis turn toward China and away from the U.S., several of the smaller Gulf states — notably Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar, which have also suffered from Iranian attacks — would likely follow suit. With Oman continuing to discuss a joint arrangement with Iran to manage the strait of Hormuz, only the United Arab Emirates might stand with America to confront the Iranians.

Ceding the region to China surely is not a prospect Washington should relish, even if it wishes to lower its Middle Eastern profile. For that reason, it would behoove the Trump administration to reconsider its rejection of Saudi entreaties, and, despite the materiel shortages it surely confronts, come to the aid of its longstanding Middle Eastern ally.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.body:
GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), who lost his primary to an opponent backed by President Trump, predicted a reckoning for the president and the GOP in the midterm elections.

“I think his comeuppance will happen on Election Day, and the day after I think there’s going to be a reckoning,” the Republican lawmaker said during an interview Thursday with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on “The Source.”

Massie, who was defeated in the GOP primary by Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, has been an outspoken critic of the president and his administration’s policies.

The Republican lawmaker has crossed party lines to support several Iran war powers resolutions and led a bipartisan push in the House for the release of the Justice Department’s files related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Collins asked the Kentucky Republican on Thursday specifically about the decision of several Republicans running for reelection this cycle to criticize tactics used by federal officers in the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration enforcement operations.

“I was the Republican who was speaking out for so long, and they were all whatever Trump wants, they were all for it in their primaries,” Massie said. “They’re about to take a shellacking here in the general election, so they’re running from him on this and other issues, like the war.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R), who is engaged in a tight battle in Kansas to retain his seat this November, said Thursday he expressed concerns to the Department of Homeland Security about the immigration operations and urged they be carried out in a “responsible and secure manner.”

Massie also criticized the president’s decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House for a lavish state dinner Thursday evening, saying it sends a “mixed message.”

“He will invite a communist to the White House, but I can’t even go there for the Christmas party,” the Republican said. “His retribution tour on Republicans, I think, stands in stark contrast to the way he’s treating the communist leader of China and also the mayor of New York.

“But you know, that’s just who he is,” Massie added. “He’s not an ideologue. He doesn’t have a true north, or honestly any kind of beliefs.”

articles.title: Beware of billionaires gifting Trojan horses to steal your election data
articles.summary: Earlier this month, Americans got a look inside Elon Musk’s own Trojan Horse.
articles.body:
It’s fitting that millions of Americans spent this summer revisiting “The Odyssey” and getting reacquainted with the ancient world’s most infamous trick: the Trojan horse. Perhaps it means we are all a bit more prepared to be skeptical of certain gifts.

Because earlier this month, Americans got a look inside Elon Musk’s own Trojan horse.

It’s called VoteSafe.org. On the surface, the site — operated by Musk’s America PAC — looks like a public resource designed to help Americans register to vote, check their registration or find their polling place. Underneath, it is a sophisticated political data operation.

VoteSafe.org is not new. Musk launched the site in 2024. What is new is what America PAC can do with the data it collects.

American PAC has reportedly rewritten the site’s privacy policy on Aug. 29, allowing it to share personal information such as name, age, address, email, phone number and IP address with advertisers, political organizations and other unaffiliated third parties. It can also sell “inferences” it makes from the information it collects from users, including “psychological trends, predispositions, behavior, attitudes, intelligence, abilities, and aptitude.”

That data is valuable. I know because I run Vote.org, the largest nonpartisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote technology platform in the country.

That’s exactly why we protect it. We don’t use voters’ information to support or oppose candidates. We don’t use data to manipulate your opinion or behavior. And we most certainly don’t sell voters’ data to the highest bidder.

VoteSafe.org does not exist in isolation. It is part of a broader and troubling pattern in which politically connected technology operations are moving into civic spaces that depend on public trust.

This summer, the Guardian reported that the National Design Studio — “an opaque White House office” led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia and staffed in part by veterans of Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency operation — had built a copy of the website Vote.gov on White House-controlled infrastructure. The actual Vote.gov site is supposed to be run by an independent, bipartisan commission — the Election Assistance Commission.

The proposed copycat site would have required voters to verify their identities and check their citizenship against a Department of Homeland Security database. It would also have allowed White House officials to access user data.

To be clear, that copycat site is not the Vote.gov Americans use today. According to the Election Assistance Commission, the White House effort was paused and the current public site remains on infrastructure controlled by the commission with no connection to White House systems. But given the opacity surrounding the whole thing, that official assurance does not resolve every question about where data may flow on the backend.

This episode should concern anyone who cares about trustworthy elections. Congress placed federal election assistance in the hands of an independent, bipartisan commission — not the White House — for a reason. Moving voter registration services onto infrastructure controlled by any sitting president would blur an important line between neutral election administration and partisan political power. It would also raise serious questions about what information is collected, who can access it, and how it might be used.

VoteSafe.org and the National Design Studio are both examples of political operations trying to assert control over machinery voters depend on to participate in our democracy — and that’s incredibly dangerous.

This is exactly why the work of organizations like ours that provide independent, nonpartisan resources with accurate and credible information to voters with no ulterior motives matters so much right now. Voters shouldn’t have to trade their personal information just to find out how to register or where to vote. And they shouldn’t have to wonder whether the voting website in front of them is a neutral public service or a political operation angling for their data.

They should be able to trust that the site in front of them is what it claims to be, and not a Trojan horse.

articles.title: Supreme Court, over liberal dissents, lets DHS overhaul immigration database for midterms
articles.summary: The Supreme Court cleared the way Friday for the Trump administration to implement its overhauled immigration database, which it says is aimed at combatting voter fraud, in time for November’s elections over the dissent of the liberal justices. The overhaul faced opposition from Democrats and some voting groups, and a judge had blocked it for violating…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court cleared the way Friday for the Trump administration to implement its overhauled immigration database , which it says is aimed at combatting voter fraud, in time for November’s elections over the dissent of the liberal justices.

The overhaul faced opposition from Democrats and some voting groups, and a judge had blocked it for violating federal privacy law. The Supreme Court’s emergency ruling lifts that block, finding the challengers’ claims are likely to fail.

The majority wrote that “the Federal Government has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters.”

“The order below prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court wrote.

The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) service is used to determine eligibility for certain federal programs.

The DHS made significant updates after President Trump directed the agency to ensure election officials had appropriate access to verify their voters’ citizenship. The changes connect SAVE to Social Security records, among other updates.

The three liberal justices publicly dissented, led by Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson.

“In my view, however, the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” Jackson wrote, joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan.

It is not a final ruling, but the justices’ order means the overhaul can proceed for the midterms as the litigation continues. The case now returns to the lower courts.

The dispute is among election-related emergency litigation that has swarmed the Supreme Court in the lead-up to the midterms.

Trump’s win comes just days after the court ruled against him on his mail-in voting plan . And days earlier, the court ruled against Missouri Republicans by lifting a judge’s directive to proceed with their new congressional map. That case has now returned to the justices once again.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the Supreme Court that the SAVE overhaul is needed to protect election integrity.

“DHS’s SAVE system was not up to the job because it lacked comprehensive data about natural-born citizens, permitted searches only one record at a time, and required the user to supply a person’s alien registration number (or other DHS number)—which States often do not know,” Sauer explained.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, an appointee of former President Biden, blocked it in June. She found the changes violated the Social Security Act and a federal law that regulates how the government can disclose individuals’ personal data.

The Trump administration brought her ruling to the Supreme Court after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to lift her order in a 2-1 vote.

Voting groups called the overhaul “unprecedented” in their filings with the Supreme Court and urged the justices to not get involved.

“Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” the League of Women Voters said in a statement. The group is leading the lawsuit.

“However, this case is not over,” the statement continued. “The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands.”

articles.body:
President Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for their visit to the U.S., saying “great strides” have been made without giving any details.

“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we’ve really enjoyed it,” Trump said at the tea ceremony in the White House’s Red Room. “And I think we’ve made tremendous strides. We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”

He also thanked the media for the “fair coverage” of the Chinese leader’s visit amid a battle with the press in which Trump had sought to block access for three organizations over their coverage of him.

Trump said he thinks U.S. farmers “are going to be very happy” because of the visit, but didn’t provide details for why.

“A lot of very positive things happened, but America is very happy about this visit, and I’m sure China is very happy also,” he said. “Great things for both countries, and it’s been just very, very productive.”

Xi, for his part, invited Trump and first lady Melania Trump to visit China. Trump traveled to Beijing in May to meet with Xi, but the first lady did not attend.

The Chinese leader said that during the May visit, he and Trump “agreed on the vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.”

“This time, we’ve agreed to add new substance to it, that the relationship will be a constructive one of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity,” he said.

He also noted that he and Trump will see each other twice more this year — during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in November and the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.
